#2624. Takeaways from College Football Week 11: Wake Forest is for real, Georgia reigns supreme

College football is unpredictable and delightful, which is why we live for what happens on Saturdays. And Week 11 delivered, from a lopsided victory in Dallas to a last-second comeback in Baton Rouge and everything in between.

Each Sunday, I'll publish my biggest takeaways from the college football weekend. I'll highlight the most interesting storylines, track College Football Playoff contenders, and specifically shout out individual and team performances that deserve the spotlight.

The Demon Deacons continue their assault on the ACC. They've beaten their last five ACC opponents by an average of 39.6 points, and they certainly made a point with the way they jumped all over SMU on Saturday, just two days after Wake Forest coach Jake Dickert signed a long-term extension. With a 42-0 lead at halftime, Dickert told radio sideline reporter Dave Goren, "We're not finished with them yet. We came for 60 minutes, and they've got nowhere to hide" — an all-time great coach quote from the midst of a beatdown. But this was clearly a message sent to the College Football Playoff selection committee, which hasn't been ranking the Deacs high enough to make the 12-team bracket so far.

Why Wake Forest is a College Football playoff team

The College Countdown crew breaks down Wake Forest's latest win, and why the team needs to be taken seriously, and question how far their offense can bring them in the postseason.

I feel like so much of the (mis)perception of Wake Forest is due to preconceived notions everyone had about the ACC coming into the season. Outside of Miami, people talked up Louisville and SMU, neither of which turned out to be anything close to the second-best team in the league. It's taken everyone too long to give the Deacs their due. Not me, though! I've had them on my AP ballot since Week 4. Give Gio Lopez and Carlos Hernandez their rightful due!

The Bulldogs have looked like the very best team in college football after the rather inexplicable loss to Auburn. In the three SEC games since that upset, Georgia has won its games by an average of 27 points. Georgia has been dominant on both sides of the ball, balanced on offense and its usual salty self on defense. Ole Miss got a taste of it a week ago, and Missouri became Georgia's latest victim on Saturday.

Joshua Perry, Ahmed Fareed, Chris Simms and Nicole Auerbach all agree that Georgia is the best team in college football right now.

LSU did not spend all that money — and disrupt the entire sport's ecosystem — to go 8-4. And 8-4 would be a best-case scenario at this point! Lane Kiffin's squad is currently 6-4 after losing back-to-back games in fairly excruciating fashion, first to rival Alabama and then to Texas in the final seconds. Kiffin is now 5-19 (!) vs. top-ten teams as a head coach. He's a pretty good head coach but not one of the game's best, and he doesn't get the most out of his teams in their biggest moments. I think the best word to use to describe Kiffin's debut season in Baton Rouge is this: Disastrous.

Curt Cignetti took some time this week to complain about the College Football Playoff selection committee after the Hoosiers dropped five spots after a bye. But this committee has been pretty consistent in its messaging. It loves big wins and will excuse (or discount) losses as long as there are signature wins to offset them (particularly in the SEC). Indiana has been shaky offensively for much of the year — but not against USC's defense on Saturday. Grant Wilson threw for more than 300 yards and two touchdowns in his first Indiana start, and Indiana got its first win over a team the committee has in its Top 25.

Cignetti backed up CFP criticism with win over USC

Joshua Perry, Ahmed Fareed, Chris Simms and Nicole Auerbach debate Curt Cignetti's comments about Indiana's rankings, and break down the Hoosiers' big win over the USC Trojans.

I said a few weeks ago that we were about to find out just how good these Wildcats are. They were 7-1 heading into their final stretch of SEC play — Tennessee, Florida and Missouri in three consecutive weeks. And, it turns out, the season-defining stretch did define the season for Kentucky. Saturday's loss to unranked and reeling Florida followed a blowout loss to Tennessee. These back-to-back losses brought the Wildcats' record to 7-3 and very likely knocked Kentucky out of the CFP.

Kentucky is still in great hands with Will Stein. It's been a fantastic Year 1, and the program is trending in the right direction. But this season is not going to end with a historic CFP berth.

You've got the best player in the sport (Jeremiah Smith) on a team that is wildly disappointing without its starting quarterback and likely won't be playing on conference championship weekend. The potential top quarterback in the 2027 NFL Draft (Drew Mestemaker) is on a team that's not a CFP contender, which might mean voters aren't watching him closely. CJ Carr is playing for a Notre Dame team that doesn't have any ranked opponents left, so he also may not attract a ton of eyeballs down the stretch (and he, too, won't be playing in a conference championship game).

Darian Mensah is hanging around — and Miami will almost certainly play in the ACC title game — but he lost to another Heisman Trophy contender in South Bend. Maybe Gunner Stockton gets some love as Georgia continues to bulldoze its way through the SEC? Or the electric Devon Dampier, whose Utes should play for a Big 12 title? Could either of those players make up some ground with some marquee opportunities ahead? It's possible. It's a weird (and weirdly quiet) Heisman race that seems to be missing buzz and big moments. But maybe I'll be proven wrong in the weeks to come!

The Bruins are 10-0. Yes, you read that right. Bob Chesney has totally flipped the script at UCLA in just one season. The Bruins went 3-9 a year ago and have already completed the greatest one-year turnaround in program history. But! They're not done yet. They've got a trip to Michigan and a home game against crosstown rival USC before an expected trip to the Big Ten championship game. Still, it's safe to pencil the Bruins into the CFP at this point — and rewrite 'em in ink if they get one more win — especially when you look around and see the number of losses taken already by so many of the other CFP contenders. And what an achievement that is for Chesney and co.

Another embarrassing on-field performance. Another week with foot-in-mouth comments to the media. It's just not working out, and there's nothing to really build on. What's there to get fans or donors excited about Year 2?

Could Whittingham be one-and-done at Michigan?

Nicole Auerbach and Joshua Perry play "Imagine That," debating whether Kyle Whittingham could be one-and-done at Michigan and whether Lane Kiffin's first season at LSU could end with five losses.

#2620. LSU’s Lane Kiffin fell to his knees after QB Sam Leavitt threw endzone INT in close loss to Texas

LSU Tigers head coach Lane Kiffin had a fairly dramatic reaction to QB Sam Leavitt throwing his third interception of the night.

Kiffin and the Tigers knew they basically needed to go undefeated for the rest of the regular season to have a chance at earning a spot in the College Football Playoffs, but they were also up against a dangerous Texas team in the same boat.

Texas picked up a 22-21 win with a game-winning TD with less than five seconds left on the clock, putting a moment from Kiffin in perspective when the Tigers missed out on a chance to put the game away.

In the third quarter of the clash, Leavitt had the opportunity to help the Tigers convert a touchdown with a pass to WR Jackson Harris in the endzone, but the pass was stolen by Texas WR/CB Jermaine Bishop Jr., prompting Kiffin to close his eyes and fall to his knees.

The Tigers missed an opportunity to extend their in-game lead to over 10 points in an electric first quarter. Leavitt ended the game 27/37 on pass attempts for 244 yards and two touchdowns, but this was his third thrown interception of the clash.

Leavitt did outplay Texas QB Arch Manning in many respects, but Manning successfully threw the game-winning TD when it mattered most and ended with 19/36 on pass attempts for 174 yards and one TD, along with three INTs.

This was the first ranked SEC matchup since 2000 where both QBs threw three INTs, highlighting that neither QB had an especially successful evening.

Coach Kiffin will be devastated by this loss, as the 6-4 (3-4 vs. SEC) Tigers would need a miracle run at this point to earn a spot in the CFP, while Texas keep their hopes alive for another week.

#2619. Practical, possible, and unlikely trades for Jalen Green

The Phoenix Suns are starting to work things out.

Winners of five of their last six, after a 1-5 start, the team is now 5-6 and recently beat the streaking Houston Rockets after outplaying them down the stretch. However, questions remain about starting guard Jalen Green's fit as he continues to average career lows as a scorer and from three, and the team is lacking a starting-level point guard alongside Devin Booker.

Questions have further arisen about his future in Phoenix after NBA Insider Chris Haynes reported Friday that the Suns have interest in acquiring point guard Dejounte Murray from the Pelicans, who recently requested a trade. With the two making similar amounts, the teams could trade them for each other without including any additional salary. But with heightened expectations after a surprising 2025-2026 campaign, the Suns could be looking to deal Green to more than just New Orleans to help their point guard problem. His $36 million salary gives the franchise some flexibility if they can find a good trade partner.

A common trade structure, the aforementioned deal is a classic "my problem for your problem" type of deal. Similar to the Cleveland Cavaliers and Los Angeles Clippers swap of Darius Garland and James Harden back in February, Green and Murray fit each other's situation better than their current ones.

Now 30 years old and coming off a torn Achilles, Murray better fits a team looking to compete for the playoffs this season, and since Joe Dumars and Troy Weaver took over leadership in New Orleans, the Pelicans have been acquiring young players such as Jermiah Fears and Derik Queen to build for the future.

With rumors continuing to heat up about both guards' futures, this seems like the most likely and easiest deal the Suns could pull off.

Bucks Receive: Jalen Green, 2027 First-Round pick (least favorable of Cleveland, Minnesota, and Utah)

While Herro would create the same problem Green does from a point-guard perspective, he's a significant upgrade and would give the Suns a more efficient, reliable scorer. With the Bucks already out most of their future picks because of their failed efforts to build a competitive roster for Giannis Antetokounmpo during his final years in Milwaukee, and potentially facing punishment for the contract they gave Gary Trent Jr., the Bucks could be looking for every opportunity to add future draft compensation.

In the last year of his four-year extension he signed back in 2022 when he was with the Heat, the Suns would likely need some assurance that Herro would be willing to stay in Phoenix before making the deal, but he would be a major talent upgrade over Green and had the same college coach as Devin Booker in John Calipari.

Trail Blazers Receive: Jalen Green, 2027 First-Round pick (least favorable of Cleveland, Minnesota, and Utah)

The Portland Trail Blazers already have too many guards, and adding another inefficient, G League Ignite alum guard alongside Scoot Henderson would not make sense for one of the league's biggest surprises through the first four weeks of the season, even if it got them a first-round pick; acquiring Holiday would make a world of difference for the Suns.

Playing alongside Booker in multiple Olympics and facing off against him in the 2021 NBA Finals, Holiday is a proven veteran playing in a bench role because of the Blazers' guard-heavy roster. He doesn't need the ball to score and knows how to win at the highest level. He's the only NBA player this decade with multiple Olympic Gold Medals and Finals victories. He's made the playoffs six straight seasons and helped both the Bucks and Celtics break their 15+ year title droughts. Many consider him to be the piece that made Boston's 2023-2024 team such a dominant one.

Who else should the Suns consider for Green?

#2618. NHL Power Rankings: Flyers flounder to start new season as Rick Tocchet searches for answers

I hate to get so negative just one week into the season, but the Philadelphia Flyers have forced my hand. After a magical run to the second round of the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, the Flyers have fallen on their face through four games.

Philadelphia opened the season with a 7-0 loss to the rival Pittsburgh Penguins, and coach Rick Tocchet described his team's play as "disturbing." There was only one way for the season to go after that, right? Wrong.

The Flyers are off to an 0-2-2 start, and the underlying numbers aren't pretty. Per Natural Stat Trick, they have a five-on-five expected goals share of 26.0%, which ranks last in the NHL. Their 4.57 xGA/60 also ranks last. Their 1.94 xGF/60? You guessed it. Last.

Tocchet's bunch entered the season with a lot of well-earned optimism. Even with subpar play from Matvei Michkov last season, the Flyers managed to reach the Eastern Conference Semifinals. Rookie Porter Martone asserted himself as a budding star with six goals and nine assists in 19 games between the regular season and playoffs.

There's still plenty of time -- 80 games exactly -- for the Flyers to get back on track and restore that optimism, but to say this has been a discouraging start would be an understatement.

#2614. Kyrie Irving was recognized in Cleveland, in honor of his Game 7 shot to secure the 2016 NBA Finals

Kyrie Irving got a moment in the spotlight during the first timeout of Saturday's game between the Dallas Mavericks (7-5) and the Cleveland Cavaliers (6-7) at Rocket Arena.

The home crowd roared in appreciation as Irving's step-back 3-pointer to seal the Cavaliers' Game 7 win over the Golden State Warriors in the 2016 NBA Finals was replayed on the video boards at midcourt.

Irving tapped his chest and thanked the crowd as the Mavs left their huddle to return to the floor with 7:32 left in the first quarter. He may not have left the Cavaliers on the best terms a season later, but that shot proved to be the clincher in the franchise's first and only NBA Championship. He asked for a trade in the 2017 offseason, and the Cavaliers sent him to the Boston Celtics in exchange for Isaiah Thomas, Jae Crowder, Ante Žižić, and a 2018 first-round draft pick.

The Cavs won Game 7, 93-89, scoring just 18 points in the fourth quarter that night. They held Stephen Curry and the Warriors to just 13 points down the stretch. Irving scored five, and someone named LeBron James had 11 as Cleveland claimed the title behind their own version of Batman and Robin.

"I wanted to prove everybody wrong, and I wanted to prove myself right," Irving said in an interview with NBA.com before the game. "What a time. Shoutout to all of my teammates that were part of that team. It was a hard-fought season. I was coming off injury, going through a lot of emotions throughout the year and just being uncertain whether I could get back to the level I believed I could get back to. After we won, I was still like, 'Is there more?' Now when I look at this [shot], there's just this appreciation of my youth, my fearlessness — things I attribute my success to today. Game 7, NBA Finals — that's the pinnacle of any player's career. "

He rose up over Curry, kept his right elbow tucked and sank one of the most historic shots in NBA Finals history as a 24-year-old that night, just five years into what has blossomed into a 15-year, Hall of Fame-worthy career. He scored 26 points and pulled down six rebounds that night, just two games after putting together a 41-point masterpiece in the Cavs' win in Game 5.

James, who scored a matching 41 points in Game 5 that year, would win NBA Finals MVP as he and Irving brought a title to his hometown team.

The Cleveland crowd also gave Irving an ovation when his name was called during the pregame introductions for the starting lineups.

#2609. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2604. Cavs beat Mavericks 127-117 behind Tyrese Proctor’s triple double

The Cleveland Cavaliers beat the Dallas Mavericks 127-117 behind an inspiring effort from their reserves.

The Cavs played on a skeleton crew tonight, with most of their usual rotation sidelined after last night's delay kept them in Miami longer than expected. Donovan Mitchell, James Harden, Peyton Watson, and Jarrett Allen all sat out while Evan Mobley, Sam Merrill, and Nae'Qwan Tomlin were out with respective injuries.

The starting lineup tonight was Tyrese Proctor, Meleek Thomas, Jaylon Tyson, Mario Hezonja, and Thomas Bryant.

The trio of Proctor, Thomas, and Tyson, who have labeled themselves as 'the pitbulls', set the tone early by being hyper-aggressive and active on both ends of the floor. They combined for 41 points in the first half, doing a little bit of everything to help build an 18-point lead going into the locker room.

Proctor finished the game with 24 points, 11 rebounds, and 10 assists. It was the strongest game of his career and proof of concept that Proctor is a foundational piece of this team's future.

Rocket Arena, which began the night feeling scorned by the stars who sat out, gave a hefty round of applause for the young group that showed up tonight.

Bryant and Hezonja deserve credit as well for serving as the veteran leaders of a younger, more inexperienced lineup. Hezonja scored 22 points on 9-of-12 shooting while Bryant added 19 points on 7-of-12 shooting.

Kyrie Irving scored 34 points and was given a warm reception both when he was announced in the Mavericks' starting lineup and after the Cavs played a video of his iconic Game 7 shot over the Warriors. It was nice to see Irving play basketball back in Cleveland.

The Cavs also saw support from two-way prospect Norchad Omier, who added 13 points and 8 rebounds by hustling around the court all night. It's performances like this that made a double-digit victory possible despite being short-handed.

Overall, the Cavs' youth showed that you can accomplish a lot by simply playing hard. The cohesion that was shown by this group tonight should be kept in mind moving forward.

Cleveland is back home on Monday against the Chicago Bulls.

#2600. The Knicks are struggling to finish games to start the season

It was just a few months ago that you could've turned a Knicks game off and celebrated within the last five minutes if it was a one-possession game: that's how automatic they were in the clutch.

Led by the former Clutch Player of the Year and an impeccable supporting cast, it seemed like every time they found themselves in a late and close situation, it was automatic after those two CJ McCollum games. Even going back further than that, this team's ability to dig deep when they need it most has been the defining characteristic of the Jalen Brunson era.

With an identical roster back in 2026-27, you'd expect it'd be the same… except it's not.

In the Knicks' 6-6 start, they've played seven clutch games. They've lost six of them.

Not all clutch games are created equal, but all of these games were winnable. Even last night's loss against Indiana, which I was saying felt like a "fake clutch game," as the Knicks got a few buckets late to make it look close, they somehow managed to have the ball with a chance to send it to overtime at the buzzer.

One way or another, the Knicks have failed to win these games. The lone win, the high-scoring thriller in Chicago, was the only game where it's felt like last season's Knicks that found a way.

Overall, in their 1-6 record in clutch games, the Knicks have a minus-17.4 net rating, ranking 22nd in the NBA. They don't do anything truly bad in these games, but they do nothing well.

Their turnover rate is league average, as is their assist rate. Their rebounding goes from dominant to so-so, but the real culprit is the putrid 50.7 TS%, which ranks 23rd. That's the catalyst behind an offense that hasn't worked in these situations.

If you exclude the Chicago game, they have a minus-40 net rating with an 82.9 offensive rating and an even rougher 44.4 TS%. All six of those games have come against the type of teams they've excelled against in postseason settings, but it just hasn't happened so far.

Going game-by-game, it's just a mess of missed opportunities.

In the season opener against Philly, the Knicks trailed by two with under three minutes to go. After giving up a dunk to VJ Edgecombe, OG Anunoby committed a back-breaking turnover in the open court that allowed Tyrese Maxey to score an easy layup. The Knicks never got closer.

The Boston game that followed it felt like a fake comeback at times, but the team got within one with 1:41 to go. While the Celtics never pulled away from there, Jayson Tatum never gave them a chance to come back with tough shot after tough shot.

The inability to get a stop, coupled with a bad moving screen by Karl-Anthony Towns in a crucial spot down three with 1:11 left doomed them to an 0-2 start.

Against Orlando, the game was tied at 91 at the five-minute mark, but the Knicks played so poorly over the next four minutes that they gave themselves no chance. On their next eight possessions, the Knicks went 0-for-3 from the field, 2-for-6 from the line, and had three turnovers.

In the NBA Cup game in Philadelphia, a stepback three from Brunson gave them a 90-89 lead with 1:32 left, but things would unravel after that. A clutch LeBron fadeaway and a triple from Edgecombe on the next two possessions hurt, but so did allowing a brutal offensive rebound after getting a stop with 12 seconds left.

Their biggest strength, rebounding, failed them.

Against Cleveland on Wednesday, it was tied entering clutch time and a one-point game with 3:26 left, but a peculiar decision to continue to blitz Donovan Mitchell at halfcourt allowed the Cavs to score on essentially every trip down.

One sequence that defined this one? Deuce McBride had a fastbreak layup down by five with 35 seconds to go, got stuffed, and Peyton Watson hit Jarrett Allen on an outlet for an and-1 to ice the game.

Then, last night in Indiana, the undermanned Pacers did everything they could to throw the game away, giving the Knicks the ball down by two with 2.8 to go. They drew up a post touch for Towns, but it didn't go.

I don't hate the idea, but I really wish they used Towns' newfound playmaking ability to their advantage by trying to free up a shooter on the right wing. If I have any criticism of this team's late-game offense for years now, it's too much isolation. There was enough time for a pass to at least be an option.

The team is shooting 38.9% in the clutch, a continuation of what's been annoyingly persistent struggles with efficiency. They haven't shot enough free throws to make conclusions there, but the regression we've seen from Towns and Brunson at the line has killed them in games where every point counts.

All told, this is something you expect to eventually reverse itself, but we're getting to the point in the season where samples are getting bigger and bigger.

At some point, they have to start executing in general and consistently play as a cohesive unit for all 48 minutes.

The Cleveland Cavaliers beat the Dallas Mavericks 127-117 on Saturday night.

While the win itself is notable — Cleveland entered the game at 6-7 and Dallas at 7-5 — the story was the players the Cavaliers won with.

Saturday night was Cleveland's second game in a back-to-back. The Cavs were in Miami on Friday night and lost 133-121. With the nationwide domestic flight ground stop lasting four hours on Friday, travel plans across sports leagues were impacted.

Cleveland's game finished after the ground stop ended, but the decision had already been made for the Cavaliers to fly back home Saturday morning. The team landed in Cleveland around noon local time, and then had a quick turnaround for Saturday night's game.

The Cavaliers ruled out all five of their usual starters. James Harden, Donovan Mitchell, Peyton Watson, Evan Mobley and Jarrett Allen were inactive ahead of the game.

This led Cleveland to start Mario Hezonja, Thomas Bryant, Jaylon Tyson, Tyrese Proctor and Meleek Thomas against a full-strength Mavericks squad.

Proctor led the way with a triple-double. He finished with 24 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists. Hezonja added 22 points, while Bryant had 19 points and 11 boards.

Cleveland's bench was shallow with only three players used, but they had an impact. Not only did the three eat up necessary minutes, but Norchad Omier had 13 points and eight rebounds, while Craig Porter Jr. added 9 points, 9 rebounds and 6 assists.

Dallas' 10-point loss against the backups didn't bring many positives, but six players finished with double-digit points, including all five starters. Kyrie Irving paced the team with 34 points, while star forward Cooper Flagg had 18 points, 8 rebounds and 6 assists.

Cleveland now gets a much-needed day off and returns to action Monday against the Chicago Bulls. Dallas has its own back-to-back to deal with and will end its three-game road trip on Sunday against the Boston Celtics.

#2591. Mavericks vs. Cavaliers Recap: Dallas struggles on the road, falls 127-117 to star-less Cavaliers

The Dallas Mavericks (7-6) fell to the Cleveland Cavaliers (7-7), 127-117 in a Saturday night matchup on the road. The matchup followed Dallas' 133-94 beatdown loss to the Minnesota Timberwolves on Thursday night. The Mavericks needed a bounce-back performance after Thursday night's blunder, and failed to take advantage of a second-string Cavaliers team.

Max Christie, Sergio de Larrea, Dereck Lively, and Tarik Biberovic were out for the Mavericks. Cleveland was without Donovan Mitchell, James Harden, Peyton Watson, Evan Mobley, Jarret Allen, and Sam Merrill. The Cavaliers sat all their top players after being unable to leave Miami until 9 a.m. due to a nationwide FAA grounding, following their 133-121 loss to the Heat. The nationwide grounding led to a call from Mitchell to cancel the game.

Kyrie Irving led the Mavericks with 34 points, six rebounds, and five assists, with 28 of those points coming in the second half. Tyrese Proctor contributed 24 points, 11 rebounds, and 10 assists, his first career triple-double, for the shorthanded Cavaliers.

The Mavericks struggled to defend the three early on, allowing Cleveland to make six threes in the first quarter, taking 58% of their shots from behind the arc. The Cavaliers, though shorthanded, had a hot hand early, allowing them to compete with the Mavericks in the first period. Caleb Martin was a bright spot for the Mavericks in this period, contributing nine first-quarter points as he continues to string together solid contributions in Dallas. Though the Mavericks couldn't stop Meleek Thomas's three-point shot early in the game, they walked into the second period at a 33-33 stalemate.

The Mavericks struggled offensively in the second period, letting their offensive mishaps affect how they defended the Cavaliers on the other end. The Cavaliers' early hot hand from behind the arc faded away in the second quarter, but they were able to go inside, as the Mavericks continued to struggle to defend them. The Mavericks needed more from Cooper Flagg in this quarter, who went 1-of-6 from the field as the Cavaliers' lead grew behind their 28-9 run in the quarter. Dallas walked into the intermission after giving up 38 points in the period, down 71-53, with a desperate need to punch back in the second half.

Dallas entered the second half uninspired to turn around its double-digit deficit, letting the lead swell to over twenty points. Dallas attempted to make a run midway through the third period, cutting the lead to 14, but continued to be unable to defend Cleveland to close the lead in any meaningful way. After a string of defensive stops, the Mavericks closed the gap with the Cavaliers, cutting the lead to 10. Irving provided a necessary 20 points in the third quarter when the Mavericks couldn't find a bucket. Even then, the Mavericks entered the fourth quarter with a 14-point deficit to dig themselves out of. The Mavericks' struggles seeped into the fourth quarter, despite everything Irving tried to do for Dallas. The Mavericks were unable to string together enough stops to fight back, falling 127-117.

Here are three takeaways from Saturday night's loss.

The Mavericks' offensive struggles continued on the road, shooting 39-of-94 from the field in the loss to Cleveland. Dallas needed someone to step up alongside Irving, but failed to take advantage of a less-talented group. This team needs more from guys like PJ Washington and Naji Marshall, who both shot poorly from the field in the loss to the Cavaliers. Off-nights from Flagg mean that someone else needs to answer the call, and the Mavericks failed to find someone to do so against Cleveland.

Cooper Flagg struggled in Saturday night's matchup with the Cavaliers, finishing with 18 points on 6-of-19 from the field. He was unable to find his shot tonight, and it felt like he was trying to force himself out of his slump by trying to draw whistles that he didn't get. He shot 0-of-6 from behind the arc tonight, though the Mavericks shot poorly from three as a whole. The Mavericks need more from Flagg, especially when facing a team missing its best players, because Irving can't be left to do it on his own. Flagg's youth showed tonight, and the Mavericks will need him to return to his All-Star-caliber self.

Kyrie Irving's 20-point third quarter gave the Mavericks a glimmer of temporary hope, with the Mavericks closing the Cavaliers' lead to 10. He was able to find his shot in this quarter, giving the Mavericks the push they needed to try to close the gap on the Cavaliers. Irving finished with 34 points, with the Mavericks needing every last one. Irving has played like an All-Star since returning from his ACL tear, and tonight was another impressive showing, coming when Dallas needed it the most. The Mavericks were unable to find anyone to step up to the plate alongside Irving and play with some shame against the Cleveland B-team.

The Mavericks are back in action Sunday, as they travel to Boston to face the Celtics at the TD Garden. Catch the tail end of the Mavericks back-to-back at 5 p.m. CT on KFAA-TV and MavsTV.

#2588. Devils bounce back with 4-1 win at Coventry

Cardiff Devils bounced back from losing at home on Friday to win 4-1 at Coventry Blaze and remain top of the Elite Ice Hockey League (EIHL).

Having been beaten 3-2 by Nottingham Panthers in Cardiff 24 hours earlier, the Devils opened the scoring after 12 minutes at the Coventry Skydome through Thomas Caron.

Brandon Estes doubled Cardiff's advantage before the first break, with the remaining goals all coming in the second period.

First, Sam Ruffin pulled a goal back for the Blaze, but two powerplay scores in under two minutes from Nolan Yaremko and Josh MacDonald secured back-to-back road victories for Paul Thompson's side.

"In the two years I've been with Cardiff this was the best we've played in Coventry," said the Devils coach.

"Powerplay was hot again tonight, we don't get too many powerplays but when we do we're converting on them.

"We're pleased to come into a place like this against a very good team and come away with the points."

The win took Cardiff to 17 points from 11 games, two ahead of Sheffield Steelers who won 6-3 at Guildford Flames on Saturday. The Steelers complete the weekend with a home game against Coventry on Sunday.

The Devils are next in action on Friday when they host Manchester Storm before travelling to face Sheffield on Sunday, 22 November.

#2587. Brewers bash champion Dodgers to brink of NLCS sweep; CBS Sports Preseason All-America team revealed

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2585. Tottenham consider January loan recall for Mikey Moore amid Rangers return talk

Expectations were high when Mikey Moore joined 1. FC Köln on loan from Tottenham Hotspur towards the end of the summer transfer window, but the 19-year-old's spell in Germany hasn't gone according to plan so far.

Moore is still waiting for his first goal in Germany, having started six of the nine games he has played in all competitions for the Billy Goats.

Given Moore's struggles to establish himself in the Bundesliga, Tottenham and Köln could agree to terminate his loan six months early in January, according to a report from TEAMtalk.

Such a move would allow Spurs to explore alternative options for the teenager in a bid to find him a destination that would be a better fit than Köln has been so far.

Moore enjoyed great success at Rangers last season, but the Scottish side are not actively pursuing a return for him. Nevertheless, should his loan spell be terminated early, both Moore and Rangers “would be forced to consider it”, the report suggests.

No decision will be made just yet, however, with Moore's form between now and the January transfer window set to influence what happens next.

#2583. UFC 334 live results, highlights, play-by-play | Gane vs. Hokit

Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) is live TONIGHT (Sat., Nov. 14, 2026) with UFC 334, taking place inside the famous Madison Square Garden in New York City, NY, streaming exclusively live on Paramount+. UFC 334's main event is a big one: Ciryl Gane vs. Josh Hokit is the featured attraction for UFC's Heavyweight crown. The co-main is a big deal, too, with Kayla Harrison vs. Amanda Nunes for UFC's women's Bantamweight belt.

The Josh Hokit experiment reaches its zenith tonight (heaven help us all) with his chance to take UFC's most valuable title from Ciryl Gane. Hokit is only 4-0 in UFC, but his wild brawl with Curtis Blaydes coupled with his demolition of Derrick Lewis on the White House lawn have landed him in MSG. The lack of depth at Heavyweight (and fresh match-ups), along with Hokit's odious persona, have also contributed to this moment.

Gane won the interim title after drubbing Alex Pereira at UFC White House. That title became legit when Tom Aspinall vacated his belt because of long-standing eye issue caused by Gane (knuckle deep!). Gane will attempt to defend a UFC belt for the first time in his career here and prove he's a deserving champ (and not just a dirty fighter).

There's history on the line in the co-main event with Amanda Nunes trying to replicate Georges St-Pierre, in stepping away from the sport at their peak and then returning a few years later and proving they are still the gold standard. Her American Top Team teammate, Kayla Harrison, will try and stop that. Harrison will be trying to show that, despite her lack of exposure in UFC, she deserves to be in the G.W.O.A.T. conversation.

Rounding out this particularly stacked main card is Caio Borralho vs. Yousri Belgaraoui, Uros Medic vs. Kevin Holland, and Bilal Hasan vs. Luis Gurule.

The featured 'Prelim' is the retirement fight of Stephen Thompson. Wonderboy draws Charles Radtke for his swansong. The Late 'Prelims' also have Drew Dober vs. Chris Duncan, Jim Miller vs. Terrance McKinney and Donte Johnson vs. Cesar Almeida.

The Early 'Prelims' have some bangers, too. They include Melquizael Costa vs. Jared Gordon, Bia Mesquita vs. Macy Chiasson, Juan Diaz vs. Alatengheili and Evan Elder vs. Samuel Sanches.

It's standard operating procedure tonight. Here's when the various portions of the latest numbered event goes live:

UFC 334's Early "Prelims" will begin at 5 p.m. ET.

UFC 334's Late "Prelims" are scheduled to start at 7 p.m. ET.

UFC 334's PLE main card goes live at 9 p.m. ET.

All of UFC 334 airs on Paramount+, which you can stream here.

Round 1: Hokit gets his first middle finger in at the face-off.

Round 1: Nunes throws some one-twos, but doesn't land then cleanly. She lands a front kick. She grows in confidence and she keeps throwing combos. She tags Harrison and Harrison is desperate to clinch. Nunes hurts her again. Harrison goes for a takedown, but can't get it. She comes up and backs away looking shell shocked. Harrison is desperate for a takedown, she can't get it. Harrison ducks under a punch and gets a single leg takedown. Nunes rolls and gets up. Harrison hits a judo throw and pins Nunes' arm, she lands punches from the top and Nunes has no way to defend them. These aren't damaging shots, but Nunes is stuck. Harrison tries to lock up a full crucifix. Nunes survives the round. Very tough to score.

Round 2: Harrison clinches early. Nunes goes for a takedown, but Harrison stays up. Nunes presses her to the fence. Harrison looks for another judo throw, but Nunes avoids it this time. Nunes lands some knees and then gets a body lock takedown. Harrison gets up and lands another throw. She has Nunes in a similar position to the first round, in a headlock on the grond where she can just wail on her. Harrison moves to side control. Harrison gets the crucifix. Nunes survives again, thanks to how light Harrison's punches are.

Round 3: Nunes lands a few punches early. Harrison clinches. Nunes fails on a takedown attempt and then backs off. Harrison tries to catch a front kick, Nunes is able to pull off a takedown from that position. She gets full mount against the cage. Harrison gets away with a fence grab. They get to the feet. Harrison is looking tired. Harrison goes for the same judo throw, again, but this time Nunes is able to land on her back and get her hooks in. Harrison turns and gets top position. Harrison lands some big elbows. That causes a cut. I think that steals the round.

Round 4: Nunes shrugs off a clinch and lands a big punch over the top. Nunes throws a front kick, Harrison catches it and tips her over. Nunes falls to the mat and Harrison jumps on her back, slaps on a rear naked choke and gets the win.

Official decision: Kayla Harrison def. Amanda Nunes by submission (rear naked choke), round 4 (1:29)

Round 1: Borralho lands a one-two. Belgaroui lands a big body kick. He misses the next two, badly. Borralho steams in and gets on the hips. He pushes Belgaroui to the fence and then drags him down. Belgaroui climbs to the fence and Borralho jumps on his back and manages to get a body triangle. Borralho lands a punch and then goes for a neck crank. Belgaroui survives that, but he's now on the ground with Borralho on his back and a lot of time on the clock. Belgaroui gets half guard, but Borralho goes for a guillotine. Borralho lands a few knees to the head as Belgaroui tries to get up. Belgaroui gets out the choke and stands. Belgaroui lands a good body kick and a blocked head kick.

Round 2: Belgaroui lands two heavy body kicks. He lands a knee as Borralho shoots. Borralho pushes him to the fence. Belgaroui gets free. Borralho lands a good right hand that stuns Belgaroui. He then shoots, but Belgaroui manages to stay up. Borralho gets the body lock and eventually gets him down, but he can't hold him there. Belgaroui is too big and strong. Borralho lands a nice combo. Borralho manages to drag Belgaroui down by the fence and get side control.

Round 3: Borralho gets a double leg takedown by the fence. Belgaroui works to his feet, but Borralho is still on him. Belgaroui goes for a guillotine and Borralho bursts out of there. Belgaroui lands a big knee to the body, both guys are very tired right now. Belgaroui brings the knee upstairs. Barralho lands a big punch. Borralho lands another big double leg, with a minute left on the clock.

Official decision: Caio Borralho def. Yousri Belgaroui by unanimous decision (30-27, 30-27, 30-27)

Round 1: Medic lands a punch of Holland's shoulder and then goes for a high kick. He misses and hits the deck. He gets up quickly and Holland is talking to him. Holland throws up some front kicks. Medic comes in and cracks him with a left hook. Holland pumps his jab and flaps his gums again. Medic falls on another kick attempt. Holland lands an uppercut shortly after. Holland leans out the way of a Medic straight and then fires back, knocking Medic down. Medic gets up, but Holland throws him down and then jumps on his neck. He goes for a guillotine, but then switches it to a D'arce. He takes Medic down and there's a minute left. Medic is able to gut it out, but Holland gets it again as Medic tries to stand. Medic is again holding on and is able to get out of it.

Round 2: Holland catches a kick to the cup. Holland takes about a minute before saying he's good to go. He's smiling and talking to Medic. Not a lot of action here, just single shots and nothing landing hard. Medic gets close and throws a combo, but Holland is able to block most of it. Holland blocks a head kick. They get close and Medic lands another kick to the cup. This time Holland takes his sweet time. Marc Goddard deducts a point from Medic and we're back on. Holland goes for a takedown, gets on Medic's back, Medic rolls and somehow ends up standing again. Holland grabs him and puts him on the fence.

Round 3: Medic catches Holland with a short counter. Holland wraps him up, possibly to get some recovery time. Holland puts Medic on the fence. He uses some knees and shoulder strikes. Medic is finding Holland's size really tough to deal with the in the clinch. Goddard breaks the clinch. They trade body kicks. Medic lands some nice shots again, but Holland is able to roll with them. Medic lands another good shot, a straight left. But Holland is able to slide back as it lands. Holland level changes right into a kick attempt and gets a shin right on his ear. He's wobbled, but Medic is very hesitant. medic tries to get the finish, but there's not enough time.

Official decision: Kevin Holland vs. Uros Medic ends in a majority draw (29-27, 28-28, 28-28)

Round 1: Hasan flashes high kicks early on, his speed is incredible. Gurule stays contained and is patiently trying to walk him down. Gurule gets close and lands a punch, but Hasan pushes him off and gets him back to kicking range. Hasan whiffs on some spin kicks. He lands a front kick to the body. Gurule blocks a switch kick and then lands a right hook that drops Hasan! Hasan bounces up again and seems fine. Gurule landed the best shot, but Hasan controlled the rest of the round. I feel a little dirty doing it, but…

Round 2: Gurule gets close enough to clinch. Hasan lands some nice knees to the body. Gurule gets him to the fence and level changes. He can't complete the takedown, though. Hasan gets back into space. Hasan lands a nice spinning kick to the body. Gurule has landed a few inside leg kicks. He's looking for that right hook again, though. Gurule ducks down and gets a double leg takedown on the fence. Gurule lands some elbows from Hasan's full guard.

Round 3: Gurule lands a short right and then transitions right to a takedown. Gurule is split open, somehow. Hasan caught him with a short elbow on the takedown. Gurule is in Hasan's half guard. Gurule lands hammerfists, desperate to avoid a stand up. Gurule has Hasan stuck to the ground, with his shoulder pressure and also his toes in the fence (which the referee is totally blind to). Gurule is beating him up.

Official decision: Luis Gurule def. Bilal Hasan by split decision (28-29, 29-28, 29-28)

Stephen Thompson vs. Charles Radtke: Wonderboy gets his walk-off moment! Radtke seemed like he had a chance to out-wrestle Thompson in the first round. He got tired quickly, though. In the second round Thompson was able to get into a groove and started to chip away with solid single shots. He almost finished Radtke at the end of the second. In the third he put him away with a spinning heel kick, making maybe the best highlight of his career.

Official decision: Stephen Thompson def. Charles Radtke by KO (spinning hook kick), round 3 (2:54)

Drew Dober vs. Chris Duncan: Duncan kept Dober at leg's length for the first two rounds with constant head and body kicks. Dober blocked most, but they succeeded in preventing Dober from blitzing forwards and starting a war. In the third round Duncan slowed down and Dober tried to get a finish, but after hurting Duncan late he gave up a takedown and Duncan was able to ride out the fight in top position.

Official decision: Chris Duncan def. Drew Dober by unanimous decision (30-27, 30-27. 29-28)

Jim Miller vs. Terrance McKinney: McKinney got to work quickly, of course. He hurt Miller with his jab, ripped a kick to the body and then landed a flush left on the chin that put Miller down. McKinney pounced with ground and pound for the win. Miller was able to tag McKinney with some counters, but he didn't have the power to stop McKinney doing what he does best.

Official decision: Terrance McKinney def. Jim Miller by KO (punches), round 1 (1:53)

Cesar Almeida vs. Donte Johnson: Johnson was very aggressive in this fight, winging punches at Almeida. They mostly found his shoulders and forearms, though. After blocking all that, Almeida landed right on the button, with a perfect straight punch, and dropped Johnson. Johnson survived the follow ups and got back to his feet. #2580. Group of retired MLB umpires, including Joe West, file lawsuit alleging they are owed more than $2 million

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Former MLB umpire Joe West is part of a group of five retired umpires who are suing their pension plan and alleging they have been underpaid by the plan, the Associated Press reports. West, along with Tom Hallion, Gerry Davis, Larry Vanover, and Jerry Layne, filed the suit in late September in federal court in New York.

The suit alleges that the five umpires have been underpaid by the pension plan by more than $2 million. According to the AP, the suit "was filed against the American Leagues and National Leagues of Professional Baseball Clubs Retirement Income Plan for Umpires and that entity's retirement committee." The five umpires claim their benefits were not calculated correctly and therefore should receive additional money.

West, 74, retired from umpiring in MLB in 2021 after umpiring more than 5,000 games at the highest level starting in 1976. The man they called "Cowboy Joe" umpired a record 5,460 games in all, was known as a colorful figure in the sport and sometimes even a source of controversy.

In 2021, West won more than $500,000 in damages as the result of a defamation suit against former MLB player Paul Lo Duca after Lo Duca alleged during a podcast that West would "open up the strike zone" for reliever Billy Wagner in exchange for driving one of Wagner's vintage cars.

West referenced his "history with lawsuits" on Thursday. From the AP:

West said that when he brought up the issue to the retirement committee, he was offered a relatively small sum. West said MLB senior vice president and chief employment counsel Steven Gonzalez told him: "If you don't like the number, sue us."

"Does Steve Gonzalez not know my history with dealing with lawsuits?" West said.

Like West, Davis also retired after the 2021 season while Hallion umpired through the 2022 season and Layne and Vanover stepped away after the 2024 campaign. The five sued as individuals and did not involve the umpires' union, their lawyer, Paul B. Holmes, said, per the AP.

A pretrial conference in the case is scheduled for Dec. 11.

#2577. Ex-Guardians catcher Bo Naylor testifies in defense of Emmanuel Clase, Luis Ortiz in MLB pitch-rigging trial

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Former Cleveland Guardians catcher Bo Naylor on Thursday testified in federal court that he perceived nothing untoward about disputed pitches thrown by former All-Star closer Emmanuel Clase and his former Guardians teammate Luis Ortiz, ESPN reports.

Naylor, who played five seasons for the Guardians, appeared as a witness for the defense in the ongoing federal trial in which prosecutors allege that Clase and Ortiz rigged multiple pitches for the benefit of co-conspiring bettors. In Clase's case, he's alleged to have done so in 17 games across a two-year period beginning in May 2023. Naylor, now a member of the Milwaukee Brewers, was catcher for some of Clase's disputed appearances during that span, including seven of the 18 pitches he's alleged to have rigged.

Naylor, a defense witness, was shown video replays of some of the pitches the government alleges were predetermined by Clase or Ortiz as part of the scheme. Naylor was behind the plate for many of them and said they looked like common sliders outside the strike zone. He said the scouting reports on the hitters Ortiz faced during the two pitches in question indicated that sliders low and away would be a "weapon."

In November 2025, Clase and Ortiz were indicted by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of New York. According to the Department of Justice, both pitchers "agreed in advance with their co-conspirators to throw specific types of pitches and speeds of pitches." The Department of Justice alleged that the pair made at least $450,000 by rigging outings and throwing specific pitches to benefit bettors who wagered on the outcomes of those pitches.

Both Clase and Ortiz pleaded not guilty to those charges in November of last year. Clase and Ortiz have been on administrative leave since late June 2025 while Major League Baseball investigates. MLB has the authority to discipline the pitchers regardless of how the criminal trial plays out.

The pair could face up to 65 years in prison if convicted on the charges of wire fraud conspiracy, honest services wire fraud conspiracy, conspiracy to influence sporting contests by bribery, and money laundering conspiracy.

#2574. Alexandra Ignatova has a new name, new title (mom) and new approach to figure skating

EVERETT, Wash. -- So much is different for Alexandra Trusova. Even her surname, which is that of her husband of two years, Makar Ignatov, in its female version, Ignatova. The Russian teenager who eight years ago led the quadruple jump revolution in women's figure skating — and reacted with childlike petulance when her record-setting five free skate quads were not good enough to win the singles gold medal at the 2022 Olympics — is now a 22-year-old woman and mother of a 15-month-old son, Mikhail. Between 2022 and now, her country has become a pariah because of its unprovoked invasion of Ukraine. She was able to start competing internationally again this season only under a special status as an "Individual Neutral Athlete."

SKATE AMERICA: Full Results | Broadcast ScheduleMotherhood gives her another special status, since she is believed to be the first mother to compete in singles skating since Japan's Miki Ando did it briefly in the 2013-14 season. She no longer is the jumping marvel known as the "Quad Queen." As a skater, she is more of a person in full, one who can interpret a program rather than simply run from jump to jump. Ignatova showed that in Saturday afternoon's short program at Saatva Skate America. A gossamer dress accentuated her flowing movement to music from the film "Lara," as choregraphed by Frenchman Benoit Richaud. "I did skate to more slow, more lyrical music before (in) one year. But now I know better how to skate to this kind of music," she said through a translator after taking second in the short to a dazzling performance by Japan's Ami Nakai, the 2026 Olympic bronze medalist. Ignatova is plainly delighted to be back in the arena, an attitude that sharply contrasted to her previous workmanlike demeanor on the ice. "Yes, I do enjoy really," she said. "Otherwise, why would I do it? "When you are young, and you don't know another life, you just do what you have been doing since you were 4 years old. You go towards your goal. Because of this, you're forgetting that you need to love what you're doing. "Therefore, when I came back, I knew that I want to do this, and I love to do this, and that's why I'm enjoying it." She has made her life something of an open book in frequent Instagram posts. She recently recounted her long trip to Everett with Mikhail from last week's Cup of China event, in which she took second, and a shopping trip here that left her wondering how she would get all her purchases back to Russia. Either her mother or husband travels with her and her son. Her mother went to China and returned home. Ignatov met her in Washington. She was disappointed to find out there would be no exhibition gala at Skate America, so there would be no chance for her to do side-by-side quadruple Lutz jumps with Ilia Malinin. He had a Lutz among three clean quads (in four attempts) while finishing second to Italy's Daniel Grassl Saturday night's free skate. Malinin wound up first overall. The Lutz is the sole quad in Ignatova's current arsenal, which had included the flip, Salchow and toe loop. For now, her free skate has one quad Lutz. She has joked that no one should expect her to do five quads in a free skate again. When even that wasn't enough to take the 2022 gold from training mate Anna Shcherbakova, it left silver medalist Trusova in a fury. "Everyone has a gold medal!" she said in Beijing. "Everyone has! Only I don't! I hate figure skating! I hate! I will never step on the ice again! Never!" The everyone in question were the Russians who had won the Olympic team event, a victory later overturned when it was learned another of her training mates, Kamila Valiyeva, had tested positive for a banned substance two months before the Olympics. Ignatova, who did not skate in the team event, later insisted that "only emotions" led her to talk of leaving the sport. She kept going the next season, the first of three in which Russian skaters would be completely barred from international competition because of the Ukraine war. She did no national competitions the past three seasons, yet clearly was ready to take advantage of the opportunity to compete again outside of Russia. "I don't try to think about (it being) a break," she said. "I know what I can do, and I worked for being able to skate well and clean, and to feel and feel myself on the ice as same as (before). Obviously, in my life everything is different now, but on the ice, it is still the same." Same old, same old includes training under the controversial Eteri Tutberidze, who had been her once and future coach. After the 2019-20 season, when she felt Tutberidze was more focused on her other top skaters, Ignatova left that training group for one directed by 2006 Olympic champion Yevgeny Plushenko. After one season, she returned to Tutberidze. One season later, she was back with Plushenko. Then, this January, back to Tutberidze. Phew. Ignatova began her comeback this season with two Challenger Series events, and a win in the second made her eligible for the Grand Prix as an alternate. Places soon opened for her in the fields for Cup of China and Skate America. A near sellout crowd at Everett's Angel of the Winds Arena greeted her warmly, some encouraging her with shouts in Russian. She skated error-free and trails Nakai by eight points going into Sunday afternoon's free skate. "It is great just to be here and to be able to perform here," Ignatova said. Philip Hersh, who has covered figure skating at the last 13 Winter Olympics, is a special contributor to NBCSports.com.

Ilia Malinin starts next figure skating chapter with a new nickname

Ilia Malinin competes for the first time this season at Saatva Skate America, live on NBC Sports and Peacock.

#2571. Connor Hellebuyck trade: Jets send star goalie to the Devils in exchange for four players, two draft picks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Connor Hellebuyck is a now a Devil. The star goalie for the Winnipeg Jets is on the move after being traded to New Jersey on Friday in exchange for four players and two future draft picks. the teams announced the move with the Jets receiving Dawson Mercer, Nick Bjugstad, Nico Daws and Alexander Command, plus a 2027 seventh-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick.

Hellebuyck expressed his desire to be traded in the offseason when he formally requested a move in August. He said at the time that he had made the request months earlier and tried to keep the situation private.

Hellebuyck has spent his entire career with Winnipeg after being drafted by the Jets in 2012 at No. 130 overall. He's recognized as one of the best goalies in the league as a three-time Vezina Trophy winner. He also helped carry the United States to its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Olympics in February with some incredible saves against Canada in the final game.

After trading Jacob Markstom in the offseason, the Devils had a clear need in goal, and this splashy move certainly fills that need. With a talented young core already in place, New Jersey's Stanley Cup window is wide open.

RAISE HELLE!Connor Hellebuyck is a New Jersey Devil: https://t.co/HCehRGOQI5 pic.twitter.com/dZGNQR16m1

For the Jets, it must be a hard pill to swallow when a franchise icon decides to walk out they door, but this trade package should help them as the enter a new era and revamp the roster. Winnipeg got a former first-rounder in Mercer to try and add to a rebuild as well as a veteran presence in Bjugstad. They also acquired a younger goalie in Daws who could fill the role of Hellebuyck at just 25 years old.

Goaltending has been an issue in New Jersey for a while now -- even after the team acquired Markstrom from the Calgary Flames in 2024. Markstom never really panned out, and his 13.6 goals allowed above average, per Natural Stat Trick, were a big reason why the Devils missed the postseason last year.

In the early portion of this season, it was clear that New Jersey needed to make a move to upgrade in the crease. Daws and veteran Jake Allen simply aren't a tandem suitable for a Stanley Cup contender, and the numbers backed that up. New Jersey ranks 24th in team save percentage at .877, and the duo of Daws and Allen combined to surrender 2.99 goals above average.

Once Hellebuyck gets up to game speed, that shouldn't be a problem anymore.

In the three-season stretch from 2023-26, Hellebuyck led the NHL with 73.42 goals saved above average, which is 20 goals higher than the next closest netminder. Over that span, Hellebuyck also posted a standard save percentage of .914 and an astronomical high-danger save-percentage of .832.

Hellebuyck carried less talented teams to the playoffs multiple times in his career. Now on a team loaded with weaponry in their prime -- Jack Hughes, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier to name a few -- Hellebuyck could be the final piece to the championship puzzle.

In terms of the acquisition cost, it was probably an easy deal for Devils general manager Sunny Mehta to make. The 2029 second-round pick is useless for a team that should be all-in now, Bjugstad is simply a depth piece and Daws now has no path to a starting role with Hellebuyck in town.

The most interesting trade chips are Mercer and Command. Mercer flashed major upside with 56 points in his second NHL season, 2022-23, but he hasn't really come close to hitting those heights again. Still, even if he has plateaued, Mercer remains a strong middle-six forward rising into his prime.

Although Command had his detractors -- and may have been over-drafted at No. 12 overall -- he was a consensus first-round pick last summer. That gives Winnipeg a potential franchise forward it can build around long-term, but New Jersey already has one of the deepest forward groups in the league, especially with the emergence of Arseny Gritsyuk and the acquisition of Luke Evangelista.

If we're looking for a 3-D chess angle of this deal, it only makes the Devils more appealing for a certain Minnesota Wild defenseman whose brothers just happen to play in New Jersey already. Grade -- A+

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: The Jets were never going to get fair value for Hellebuyck because, at his best, he's the No. 1 goaltender in the world with no equal. That type of excellence can't be replaced.

That said, Winnipeg did fairly well given the circumstances. Hellebuyck made a public trade request, and he wasn't even with the team after sitting out for the entirety of training camp. The entire league knew the Jets had to trade him.

Hellebuyck's talent created a decent market anyway, but most of the suitors were bona fide Stanley Cup contenders with little in the way of valuable draft capital, and they weren't going to knee cap the roster by sending a key player back in return.

With all that taken into consideration, Kevin Cheveldayoff got a solid return. Although Mercer's ceiling may be lower than initially thought, he's a 24-year-old forward who banks roughly 20 goals and 20 assists every season. The kicker with Mercer will be Winnipeg's ability to re-sign him before he hits restricted free agency next summer.

The addition of Command means Winnipeg now has two forwards selected in the top 12 of the 2026 NHL Draft after taking center Viggo Bjorck themselves. If both of those players deliver on their first-round pedigrees, they could be a terrific one-two punch for the team long-term.

Daws was a third-round pick in 2020, and despite playing just 13 NHL games since the start of the 2024-25 season, he should give Winnipeg a solid back up option behind Stuart Skinner. It certainly helps that Skinner is off to a great start with his new team -- and if Daws develops into a true No. 1 -- it'll be gravy.

If there's any reason to critique this deal from the Jets' side of things, it's that they didn't get premium draft capital or a surefire up-and-coming prospect. Maybe Command develops into a star, but there's no guarantee he becomes a top-six stud in the NHL.

The Jets got a lot of good stuff, but they didn't really get anything great, at least not based on what we know in the moment. Because of that, I have to ding Winnipeg a little bit. Grade: B

#2569. Five under-the-radar MLB free agents who could make a big impact next season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is a little more than a week old now and we're still waiting for the first big trade or free agent signing. That isn't unusual, though. The hot stove, like the regular season, is a marathon, not a sprint. A lockout is expected when the collective bargaining agreement ends at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, and there should be a flurry of activity before then.

We ranked the offseason's top 50 free agents, and although it is not a great class, there are dozens of quality players available. You just have to know where to look. Here now are five players who did not rank among our top 50 free agents, but would nonetheless be good options and solid pickups for teams that want to raise their floor and improve their supporting cast.

It was a tale of two seasons for the 29-year-old Bryan Abreu, who had a 5.81 ERA before the All-Star break and a 1.71 ERA after. The under-the-hood estimators, like FIP and xERA, were better in the second half as well, though Abreu lost close to 2 mph off his fastball this year and, not coincidentally, a whole bunch of swings and misses. Abreu is third in appearances and second in innings among relievers since 2022 and it's possible the workload is catching up to him. There's still enough bat-missing ability and late-inning experience here for Abreu to contribute to a contender's bullpen. It just might happen as a seventh-inning guy moving forward, not as the Moment of Truth™ reliever who pitches in the game's biggest moments.

If you're looking for a bottom of the order guy who will take walks and give you 10-15 home runs, that's J.P. Crawford. His defense, specifically his range and arm, has slipped so much in his early 30s that he's no longer a viable shortstop, though he played 33 games at third base this past season. I like him better at second base, but third base works too. Crawford gets on-base at a decent clip and won't strike out excessively, plus he's long been regarded as an excellent teammate and grade-A clubhouse guy. It seems like his time with the Mariners is over and it's for the best. Crawford can go elsewhere, play a new position, and just be part of the lineup rather than one of the faces of the franchise.

Due to injury and ineffectiveness, it looked like Sean Newcomb was on his way out of baseball two years ago. He then reinvented himself as a sinker/curveball guy and carved out a nice second phase to his career as a workhorse utility reliever who won't beat himself with walks (an early career bugaboo) and will limit hard contact in the air. Newcomb, 33, worked at least 90 innings the last two seasons while pitching in every possible role. He closed out games, worked high leverage as a setup guy, soaked up innings in long relief, and opened a few times as well. Newcomb is likely miscast as a go-to bullpen option, though he can be a valuable third or fourth option for a contender. The utility reliever is all the rage these days and Newcomb fits the profile to a T.

Now 35, Emilio Pagán was sensational after returning from a hamstring injury in July, pitching to a 1.88 ERA with 34 strikeouts and only five walks in his final 28 ⅔ innings. The downside is the same as it's always been: Pagán is exceptionally home run prone (career 1.51 HR/9), which is a bad trait for a late-inning reliever who pitches almost exclusively in close games. His fastball remains firm, though, and his splitter is an elite swing-and-miss pitch that allows him to neutralize righties and lefties. As long as you're willing to live with the home run risk, Pagán remains a capable high-leverage reliever, one who is not out of place pitching important innings for a contending team.

Platoon DHs are not the hottest commodity, but Joc Pederson fills the role about as well as anyone in the game. He's a left-handed hitter, so he's on the heavy side of the platoon, and he authored a .245/.338/.496 line with terrific ball-tracking data (exit velocity, etc.) against righties. If you must play him in the field, Pederson can stand in right field or at first base for about six innings before being subbed out for a defensive replacement. He's essentially a bat-only player, though. Pederson will turn 35 in April and he's still a powerful and productive hitter against righties and an elite clubhouse vibes dude.

#2568. What is FTP? Explaining ICC's Future Tours Program

What is FTP? Explaining ICC's Future Tours Program originally appeared on Cricket News. Add Cricket News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Cricket's master calendar is being reworked in Bali as the current cycle nears conclusion.

Debates over ODIs, WTC expansion and franchise windows could reshape the matches fans watch.

The programme has been overhauled several times since 2006, reshaping how bilateral cricket works.

Every cricket fan has come across the term FTP at some point, yet few could explain exactly how the Future Tours Programme decides which teams meet, where they play and why certain series return again and again while others quietly disappear from the schedule.

The subject is back in the headlines because the ICC held its final Board and Committee meetings of 2026 in Bali from November 11 to 15. It was the first time the governing body has met in Indonesia. The present cycle ends in March 2027, and the final plan for 2027 to 2031 was expected to be presented at this November gathering.

The Future Tours Programme is the official multi-year master calendar issued by the International Cricket Council. It maps out every bilateral international tour in Tests, ODIs and T20Is, and it places the ICC's own global tournaments alongside them across a fixed cycle that usually runs between four and five years.

Its main purpose is to bring certainty, fairness and commercial stability to the boards that play international cricket. Teams know well in advance whom they will host and whom they will visit, which allows broadcasters, sponsors, venues and players to plan their years.

The calendar also reserves protected windows for ICC events such as World Cups, the Champions Trophy and the World Test Championship final, as well as for major domestic T20 leagues like the IPL.

MORE: Former Aussie star reconfirms everyone knew about Sandpapergate

The ICC sets the broad framework, but the individual series are not handed down from above. Member boards negotiate them directly with each other, and the agreed tours are then signed off through formal Members' Participation Agreements. This means a board cannot simply walk away from a scheduled series without facing financial or legal consequences.

There isn't a single programme for everyone. Separate calendars exist for different groups of teams:

The men's FTP covers the 12 Full Members: India, Australia, England, South Africa, New Zealand, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, the West Indies, Bangladesh, Zimbabwe, Ireland and Afghanistan.

The Women's FTP covers 11 nations in the 2025–2029 cycle and runs alongside the ICC Women's Championship.

The Associate Men's FTP covers the eight nations taking part in the ICC Cricket World Cup League 2.

MORE: 30 runs in 4 innings: Sharma's poor NZ series in World Cup-like conditions a concern?

The cycle, now drawing to a close, began in 2023 and runs through March 2027.

It contains 694 international matches shared between the 12 Full Members, and it folds in both the 2023-2025 and 2025-2027 editions of the World Test Championship.

In each WTC cycle, the nine leading Test nations play six series apiece, three at home and three away.

9 teams, 6 series each (3 home, 3 away) per cycle

2023 ODI World Cup (India), 2024 T20 World Cup (USA and West Indies), 2025 Champions Trophy (Pakistan), 2025 WTC Final (Lord's), 2026 T20 World Cup (India and Sri Lanka), 2027 WTC Final

The next cycle will start in 2027 and carry through to 2031, and a number of important matters were being settled in Bali. The first concerns the future of 50-over cricket, since boards are weighing how many bilateral ODIs make sense at a time when franchise T20 competitions keep multiplying.

The second is the structure of the 2027–2029 World Test Championship, namely whether it stays a nine-team league or opens up to Zimbabwe, Ireland and Afghanistan. Reports from before the meeting indicated that proposals for the 2027–29 and 2029–31 WTC match-ups were also due to be submitted. geosuper

A third area is the balance between international commitments and franchise windows. Cricket is set to return to the Olympic programme at the 2028 Los Angeles Games, and some IPL owners have asked for a longer or winter window for their league. All of this has to be squeezed around a busy run of ICC events.

Some of the biggest bilateral commitments are already known. The Ashes will be played in England in 2027, in Australia in 2029-30 and in England again in 2031, while England are due to tour India for a five-match series in early 2028 before hosting India in mid-2029.

South Africa are also expected to host India straight after the 2027 ODI World Cup, and the BCCI has asked planners to include proper rest and acclimatisation periods, including warm-up games before major series in SENA countries. The ICC has described the process as one with many moving parts, and that description is easy to believe given how many calendars have to line up.

MORE: IPL 2027: Three teams that can sign Aaryavir Sehwag at the mini-auction

The programme has gone through four distinct phases since the ICC first introduced it, and each one reflected the priorities of cricket's administrators at the time.

The first formal FTP, launched in May 2006, required every Test-playing nation to meet every other one home and away over a six-year cycle.

After the 2014 governance reforms, the strict rotation was dropped in favour of bilateral freedom, which let India, Australia and England play each other more often in lucrative series.

Test series were linked to the World Test Championship, which began in 2019, and ODI series were tied to the 13-team Cricket World Cup Super League from 2020 to 2023.

The ODI Super League was scrapped, World Cup qualification went back to rankings and qualifier events, the nine-team WTC stayed, and more room was created for global T20 leagues.

For all the latest cricket news, opinion, and commentary, and to share your voice, head to our Facebook, Instagram, and X (Twitter) pages.
