#2444. Jake Bauers reportedly agrees to $58 million deal with Red Sox after helping lead Brewers to World Series

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Boston Red Sox have made the offseason's first major free agent signing. The Red Sox and first baseman Jake Bauers have agreed to a four-year contract worth $58 million, reports ESPN. The team has not yet announced the signing.

Bauers, 31, broke out with the World Series champion Milwaukee Brewers this past season, authoring a .266/.389/.484 batting line with 26 home runs that more than doubled his previous career high (12). He was named the NLCS MVP during Milwaukee's title run thanks to a 4 for 14 (.286) effort. Bauers drove in seven runs in the four-game sweep of the Los Angeles Dodgers.

The Red Sox desperately needed a power bat and certainly added one with Bauers. Their 163 home runs this past season were the fifth fewest in baseball and three players -- Wilyer Abreu, Willson Contreras and Jarren Duran -- accounted for 71 of those 163 home runs. Boston's lineup figures to look something like this with Bauers now added:

That leaves Duran without a full-time position and makes a trade or even a non-tender more likely. Franklin Arias, one of the very best prospects in the minors, could debut early next season and wrestle the shortstop job away from Story. POBO Craig Breslow recently said Story is not locked in as the team's starting shortstop.

We ranked Bauers as the 12th-best free agent available this offseason, and the seventh-best position player free agent. Here's our write-up:

Rake Bauers (finally) lived up to the nickname this year and carried it over into the postseason, particularly during the NLCS. Long an exit velocity and hard-hit rate darling, Bauers fully tapped into his power in 2026 thanks to a more open stance and moving back in the box and further off the plate. That allowed him to see the ball better and get his bat into the hitting position on time more consistently. I'm not 100% sold on those adjustments solving his career-long issues with lefties, though at least there is a tangible reason to believe in his great left-on-left performance this season. Bauers can be an adventure in the field (he has played outfield in the past) and he just turned 31. A few teams will look for the next Jake Bauers rather than pay the actual Jake Bauers.

The Brewers tendered Bauers the $23.15 million qualifying offer and will receive a 2027 compensation draft pick after the first round because the contract exceeds $50 million. Because they paid the competitive balance tax, the Red Sox will forfeit their second- and fifth-highest 2027 draft picks, plus $1 million in bonus pool money for the 2027 international signing period, to sign Bauers.

Milwaukee could turn to Tyler Black and Andrew Vaughn at first base next season. Andrew Fischer, the No. 20 overall pick in the 2025 draft, slugged 48 home runs in the minors this summer and reached Double-A. He is the long-term solution at first base but is likely a year away from the big leagues. The Brewers could bring in a stopgap first baseman if they're not sold on Black.

The Red Sox went 87-75 this past season and were the second wild card team. They were swept by the rival New York Yankees in the Wild Card Series and scored only two runs in the two games.

#2442. NFL week 10 anytime TD best bets: Look for Chris Olave, Jonathan Taylor to find the end zone

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Welcome to our 10th NFL Sunday of the year! Can you believe it? This week, Kirk Cousins leads the Minnesota Vikings against Jordan Love and the red-hot Green Bay Packers, the Carolina Panthers and New Orleans Saints play an important divisional game in the Superdome, and the lead in the AFC North is up for grabs when the Pittsburgh Steelers and Cincinnati Bengals take the field on "Sunday Night Football."

Let's discuss some anytime touchdown bets. These have become popular wagers among football fans because of their longer odds. Even when it comes to an expected TD scorer, they make for a fun parlay leg. Below, we will break down five anytime TD bets to consider. These will not be predictable choices like a Jahmyr Gibbs or Bijan Robinson score that offer zero value, but they won't be wild long shots such as a team defense. Let's begin with a running back.

Bhayshul Tuten is the lead back for the Jacksonville Jaguars, but he missed two practices this week with ankle and foot injuries. Chris Rodriguez Jr. is the goal-line back, and he's scored touchdowns in two consecutive games despite receiving just 16 rushing attempts.

With the Jaguars facing the lowly Tennessee Titans this week, Rodriguez should get another chance at a goal-line touchdown -- which could come much easier since Jeffery Simmons is no longer on that defensive line. Or, maybe Rodriguez gets more touches if this is a blowout.

Chris Olave has registered under 100 yards receiving in four straight games after beginning the season with 100 yards in three of his first four games. He's recorded just two receptions of 20+ air yards over the last four games, which is surprising. We predict Olave gets back on track this week against the Panthers secondary, which allowed Bo Nix to have one of his best outings of the season last week, and got diced up by Christian Watson and Matthew Golden the week prior. Olave has scored touchdowns in each of his last two games against Carolina.

I don't love suggesting a -120 touchdown scorer, but I like this situation for Jonathan Taylor. He can finally exhale now that the trade deadline has officially passed, and this week, his Indianapolis Colts host one of the worst teams in the NFL that is starting a quarterback who has never taken a snap in an NFL game before. Taylor scores on Sunday.

Here's an interesting flier. Keenan Allen played the Dallas Cowboys last Sunday when he was still with the Colts. After he was traded to the San Francisco 49ers on Tuesday, Allen will play the Cowboys again this Sunday!

Mike Evans won't play again this week, but Deebo Samuel is back. Allen just got to town, but I can see Kyle Shanahan utilizing him like he did Evans earlier in the year in the red zone. This is my long shot of the week.

One of my favorite bets I made this year was for Tee Higgins to score a touchdown against the Steelers in Week 3. He was already off to a hot start at that point, and had actually caught touchdowns in each of his last two games vs. Pittsburgh. Sure enough, he cashed at +175 with six catches for 90 yards and a touchdown. Higgins has caught six touchdowns in eight games this season! He and Ja'Marr Chase are virtually unguardable, as this dynamic duo has caught 47 passes for 693 yards and eight touchdowns over the last three games. You can take Chase to find the end zone at -120, but I'll opt for the plus money. This Bengals team is on an absolute roll, having scored at least 34 points in three straight games. I'll keep riding this passing attack.

"After taking time to reflect on my recent social media posts and speaking with people I trust and respect, I recognize that I should have been more thoughtful about what I shared on my platform.

"I realize that this content caused hurt and I sincerely apologize. I should have been more thoughtful about what I shared, recognizing the responsibility that comes with having a public voice.

"As a man of faith, it is my belief that every person deserves to be treated with dignity and respect, regardless of their religion, background, or beliefs. After hearing feedback from those I hurt, I realize that the content I shared fell short of my own convictions.

"I would like to affirm my respect for the Muslim community and for the dignity and freedom of people of every faith and background.

"From this experience, I have learned to ensure that none of my communications promote hate or give the impression that I support hatred, discrimination, or violence against anyone."

The club had earlier released a statement on the incident that read:

"Baseball is for everyone, and the Blue Jays have created an inclusive experience where all fans feel welcome at our ballpark. Individual comments do not represent our organization's values and beliefs."

Santander, a Venezuela native, shared social media videos following the recent U.S. midterm elections, including one in which a Christian pastor said, "There is no such thing as kind Muslims." Another suggested that Sharia law would be imposed in the U.S. following the election of Abdul El-Sayed to the Senate representing the state of Michigan.

Atkins told reporters Tuesday that Santander's behavior "did not align" with organizational values and there were no words "to express my level of disappointment."

"I talked to Anthony about his lack of awareness, realizing that he has a very large microphone, what that meant," Atkins said. "We're working exceptionally hard internally to ensure, and we have been, that it's a safe environment, that baseball is for everyone. It's very important to us. It's a part of our organizational values and his behavior did not align with that."

Santander, 32, joined the Blue Jays prior to the 2025 season on a five-year, $92.5 million free-agent contract. He struggled badly across 54 games in 2025 and missed the entire 2026 season with injury.

#2440. Dejounte Murray landing spots: Three possible destinations after Pelicans guard requests trade

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

We have our first trade request of the 2026-27 NBA season. If you had Dejounte Murray on your bingo card, congratulations. The 2022 All-Star landed with the New Orleans Pelicans before the 2024-25 season, but his tenure there has been a mess and he requested a trade on Friday. He played 31 games in his first season, shooting worse than he ever had before tearing his Achilles. He returned late last season and played well, but the beginning of this season has been a mess.

Murray has remained in the starting lineup for the Pelicans, but New Orleans is 1-8 in the games he's played. They've lost his minutes by over 14 points per 100 possessions, he's shot poorly from basically everywhere on the floor, and he hasn't been a consistently impactful defender since he played for the San Antonio Spurs.

Meanwhile, Murray has made his displeasure public on several occasions.

At this stage, Murray's trade value is likely minimal. If a deal comes, it will likely involve a similarly bloated, multi-year contract attached to a player that a team is eager to move. Essentially, we're looking for "problem for problem" type of trades.

Three destinations make some degree of immediate sense.

The Suns are the first team to register known interest, according to Chris Haynes. Earlier this season, Haynes reported that the team's lack of a point guard had created frustration in the locker room. Phoenix started the season 1-5, but has since won four of its last five to somewhat right the ship.

Still, the Jalen Green experience has been a borderline disaster for Phoenix. The Suns have a staggering -15.7 net rating when Green plays and a +10.2 net rating when he sits. The former No. 2 overall pick was one of the primary pieces returned in the Kevin Durant trade, but his shooting has fallen off a cliff. He provides none of the playmaking that Devin Booker needs in a backcourt mate (which is part of why the Suns have fared so much better with Collin Gillespie on the floor in his place), and his defense is mostly nonexistent.

Both Murray and Green have player options for next season, with Green set to make $36 million and $30 million owed to Murray. The notoriously stingy Pelicans might insist on some form of compensation for taking on that extra money, but the premise here would essentially be the "problem for problem" structure we suggested above. With Murray gone, Jeremiah Fears could be the unquestioned starting point guard for the Pelicans. Green would either come off the bench or slot next to him at shooting guard, while Murray would be closer to the point guard archetype that Booker prefers.

It's by no means a perfect fit. Murray's weakness as a 3-point shooter would be problematic as the Suns have lost quite a bit of shooting since last season, and the Pelicans frankly have too many talented, shoot-first players as is. But it's at least an attempt at addressing real issues for both sides. The rebuilding Pelicans might at least like to take a look at a supremely gifted athlete, while the Suns would hope to get the point guard they feel they've lacked.

Andrew Wiggins has really struggled to fit into the new, Giannis Antetokounmpo-centric version of the Heat. The former No. 1 overall pick is averaging less than nine points per game on some of the worst shooting numbers of his career. His usually steady defense has slipped a fair bit on a unit that has been enormously disappointing as a whole, and, offensively, Miami's lack of a genuine shot-creating guard has proven problematic early in the season.

The Heat need a more reliable shot-generator than Murray, but after spending most of their assets on Antetokounmpo, their options are somewhat limited. This sort of swap would essentially be a bet that going from one of the NBA's worst organizations to one of its best could rejuvenate a former All-Star. Fitting a point guard that shoots poorly from deep on a Giannis team would be pretty problematic, but Miami would presumably stagger the two of them to limit their minutes together.

Such a swap would appeal to New Orleans for a few reasons. The first is contractual. Wiggins signed an unusual contract last offseason. He had a player option for the 2026-27 season, but rather than decline it and sign an entirely new deal, he picked it up and added a cheap two-year extension on the back end. He is making over $30 million this season but will dip to $16.3 million next season. That makes him an ideal trade target for a team that wants to save money. He can match salary with Murray in a trade now, but cost far less next year.

And then of course, there's the chance that Wiggins bounces back on a team that plays a bit more traditionally than Antetokounmpo-led teams can. Pelicans wings Trey Murphy III and Herbert Jones have been rumor mill fixtures for years, and with Saddiq Bey in place and a potentially rejuvenated Wiggins incoming, New Orleans would potentially feel a bit more comfortable cashing one of those other forwards out for draft picks since they'd have replacements in the building.

Murray is emphatically not the sort of player that the Hornets tend to target, especially at point guard. Charlotte wants to bomb 3-pointers. That is not now, nor has it ever been Murray's game. When Charlotte traded LaMelo Ball, it expected to be able to sustain a somewhat respectable offense with Coby White in his place and Kon Knueppel ascending. Well, Ball is starring in Minnesota and White and Knueppel have barely played.

The Hornets knew they were taking a step back this season with the Ball trade. They probably didn't expect the NBA's worst offensive rating, highest turnover rate and lowest true shooting percentage. Bringing in Murray could at least provide them with a stabilizing force at point guard, someone who could raise the floor enough to properly evaluate everyone else on the team moving forward.

The Hornets have a $40.8 million trade exception generated from moving Ball and almost $30 million in room below the tax line. They could nearly absorb Murray outright without sending out another contract, and they've shown a willingness to take on salary in exchange for draft capital. That would be the idea here.

The Hornets are not taking on Murray's player option for next season lightly. The Pelicans would have to make it worth their while with some form of first-round draft compensation. The Pelicans are probably hesitant to do so after all of the criticism they (justifiably) received for the Derik Queen trade, but Charlotte is probably the only team that can offer real financial relief for Murray at this point. If that's a priority, there might be a conversation here. If the Pelicans expect the Hornets to treat Murray as a real asset, the Hornets almost certainly pass.

#2439. U21 European Championship Final: English Manipulation of the German Pressing – MH

von Next Generation am 06.07.2025 in den Kategorien National Teams mit 1 Kommentar

England wins the U21 European Championship final against Germany 3-2. After just 20 minutes, England leads 2-0. This aspect analysis focuses on the reasons behind the German attacking press’s lack of access to England’s build-up play.

The U21 European Championship final offered several interesting tactical elements. This analysis focuses on Germany’s lack of access in their attacking pressing and marking. Particularly in the first half, England repeatedly managed to bypass the German press, often gaining large amounts of space in the final third, which led to dangerous scoring opportunities.

The early deficit also contributed to Germany being unable to focus, as they usually do, on securing depth in their pressing. Instead, they were forced to put direct pressure on the ball carrier in order to force turnovers. After the equalizer to make it 2-2, Germany noticeably pressed high less frequently. Therefore, this analysis examines Germany’s pressing and marking, as well as England’s build-up play, up to the 60th minute.

One of the trends at the U21 European Championship was that many teams aimed to press the opponent’s goal kicks with a +1 player on the last line or in the space between the lines just in front of the back line. Many teams—including Germany—used man-oriented marking when closing down during goal kicks.

Since most teams build up from a 1-4-2-4 structure on goal kicks, it is equally common to press man-to-man from a 4-1-3-2 shape, with the two holding midfielders (the “sixes”) staggered vertically.

The deeper-lying holding midfielder (for Germany: Martel) acts as the +1 player, positioning himself in space based on the location of the ball. When the opponent plays through the space between the lines, he can create a numerical advantage there. In the final third, pressing is carried out against a 1-4-2 build-up using a 3-2 shape. The more advanced holding midfielder (for Germany: Reitz) typically positions himself centrally and marks the ball-near holding midfielder, while the far-side winger presses the ball-far holding midfielder.

The English side, by contrast, caused problems for the German team’s marking assignments through an asymmetrical structure. As a result, England had several options for exploiting their numerical superiority in the build-up without having to immediately play into the space between the lines.

What remained consistent was the intention to establish central possession in front of the first pressing line using different players, in order to build up play on either side. Central possession makes it more difficult for the pressing team to steer the play in a specific direction, as the passing angles from central areas are wider than those from more advanced or wider positions.

Central possession complicates the opponent’s shaping of play. Anderson’s drop frees him from Woltemade’s marking shadow and creates a numerical advantage against Nebel, who must now cover both the advanced full-back and Anderson.

The asymmetry in England’s build-up play also allowed them to repeatedly exploit their numerical superiority in specific areas tailored to Germany’s pressing structure. By stretching the positioning of their two holding midfielders (the “sixes”), Reitz was forced to cover too much ground to mark both or to shift quickly to the ball-near midfielder.

Because Germany, for the reasons mentioned above, struggled to steer the press in a specific direction, Reitz was also unable to position himself closer to the ball-near player during goal kicks. Instead, he was forced to choose which of the two midfielders to mark man-to-man.

The wide, asymmetric positioning of the holding midfielders and advanced full-backs makes both midfielders available for passes, forcing Reitz to choose whom to mark. German forwards can’t shadow the opposing midfielders, while German wingers must decide between marking the spaced-out midfielders or full-backs.

England’s positional rotations during build-up play after goal kicks were most often initiated by holding midfielder Anderson. When Germany applied pressure (as shown in the diagram above), Anderson would frequently drop into the right half-space, almost into a right-sided centre-back position, while fellow holding midfielder Scott positioned himself more centrally, and No. 10 McAtee dropped into the higher left half-space.

When Anderson instead dropped centrally in front of the goalkeeper, the right centre-back would shift wide, which in turn affected the positioning of other central players and full-backs. The specific rotations of the key players, including their reference points and triggers, are discussed in more detail in the section on England’s build-up against Germany’s high pressing.

A key aspect of England’s build-up against Germany’s pressing was their ability to evade pressure through these rotations. Since Germany used man-oriented marking, they followed the English players during these movements, which repeatedly opened up spaces that England could then exploit. For example, when McAtee dropped deep into the far-side half-space, it pulled Martel—who was defending space-oriented in the center—out of position.

The aim was to repeatedly open up central areas by drawing German players out of the middle. When the full-backs, due to the rotations, were positioned deep and wide in possession, the ball-near holding midfielder would shift outward, thereby opening the central channel. This would often be followed by an overlapping run by the full-back into the half-space, allowing him to be found deep in the center with his marker behind him and plenty of space to operate.

Luring central players out of position and opening up space through rotations is one of the core principles of England’s build-up play. It significantly disrupted Germany’s ability to gain access through their man-marking approach during pressing.

Holding midfielder Anderson’s run outward opens the center, which can then be exploited by the full-back’s typical forward run.

England also added flexibility by repeatedly using long balls from their build-up play. Especially when both the full-backs and the holding midfielders were positioned deep, they opted for long passes as soon as Germany’s wingers and central players were lured far enough out. The 2–0 goal resulted from one such long ball, which was held up by striker Stansfield and laid off to the advancing Elliott and McAtee in the half-space, who now had plenty of room to operate in the open central area.

Although these long balls weren’t always as successful as in the lead-up to the 2–0, they had the effect of preventing Germany from pressing too aggressively, as players had to remain ready to cover depth in case of another long ball. For example, Martel pushed forward only hesitantly toward the dropping No. 10 McAtee, giving him significantly more time on the ball in central areas.

Against man-oriented marking systems, it is particularly important to apply intense pressure on the ball carrier, since progression is otherwise easier than against a zonal setup.

As described, England repeatedly managed to exploit their numerical advantage in the build-up. However, Germany’s pressing approach also contributed to their lack of access. The primary aim of Germany’s pressing when closing down is less about disrupting the build-up itself, and more about winning the ball in a way that immediately creates a transition opportunity.

To do so, Germany tries to use its forwards to immediately block passing lanes to the flanks, forcing the play through the third man or central passes.

Recovering possession through intercepting a pass has the advantage over winning a tackle in that it tends to allow better control of the ball and therefore more often leads to a transition opportunity. Additionally, central ball recoveries naturally result in a shorter route to goal and, statistically, in higher-quality chances in front of goal.

However, this type of pressing also means less pressure is placed on the ball carrier, since the focus is on directing play and winning the ball after a pass. As a result, England’s ball carriers had more time to locate the free +1 player, made available through asymmetry and rotations.

In hindsight, it might have been more effective to place greater emphasis on actively disrupting the build-up itself, because England repeatedly managed to bypass the German press dangerously. At the same time, Germany had the ability to control the game through their own possession, so it wasn’t absolutely necessary to rely on winning the ball high up the pitch to create chances.

Germany’s attacking pressing operated on principles similar to those of their closing down (Zustellen). From a 4-4-2 formation with a slightly advanced Reitz on the left half-space, the forwards aimed to channel the opponent’s build-up play out wide in order to isolate the wide build-up players and engage them in man-to-man marking.

On the last defensive line, Germany aimed to maintain a +1 numerical advantage, which is why the far-side holding midfielder was usually responsible for covering depth. The German wingers were expected to track back from the full-backs to press the half-backs in the three-man defensive line that frequently formed.

Even when applying attacking pressing from open play, Germany was rarely able to gain effective access to England’s build-up. This was primarily due to England’s positional play during build-up. England’s main objective in possession is to lure opponents out of position and then exploit the spaces that open up. This goal is achieved through positional rotations that make it especially difficult for the opponent to apply effective pressure on the ball carrier during pressing. The frequency of these rotations strongly resembles the rotation-heavy positional play famously associated with Paris Saint-Germain.

The following outlines the key running paths, rotations, and reference points of the most important players.

The center-backs were rarely involved in the rotations. Only when one of the holding midfielders dropped into the build-up line did the center-backs position themselves wider. Likewise, striker Stansfield provided a fixed presence in the central deep-lying position.

Most rotations initially originated from the holding midfielders, particularly Anderson. Most frequently, he dropped into the right half-space just ahead of the center-backs. This caused the right full-back to position wider and winger Elliott to drop deeper into the half-space at the level of the last defensive line. As a result, Woltemade and Nebel had to press two players, creating a 3 vs. 2 overload.

There were also occasions when Anderson dropped into the central center-back position. Consequently, the full-backs rotated into the half-spaces, or No. 10 McAtee dropped deeper. Notably, Anderson could be found almost anywhere on the pitch. At times, he overloaded the far side, which was then followed by a role swap between him and holding midfielder Scott.

Holding midfielder Scott often positioned himself in spaces that were left vacant after a sequence of rotations. Usually, Scott remained central or rotated roles with holding midfielder Anderson. It also happened that Scott took up an open full-back position when both the winger and the full-back rotated deep.

A particularly noticeable tendency of both holding midfielders was that, when in possession, they rotated toward the flank if a wide player was positioned close to the first build-up line, making themselves available along the sideline. This had the advantage of stretching the center even further.

This was especially important because England frequently won second balls after losing possession in build-up play. In the resulting transition situation, the central area was completely free, leading to several dangerous counter-attacks through the now open middle of the pitch.

Livramento, as the right full-back, primarily oriented himself around Anderson and the right winger Elliott. In relation to Elliott, Livramento always behaved in a complementary manner: when one occupied the wide position, the other took up the half-space. It was also common for Livramento to invert and drop into the deeper half-space, with Elliott moving wider in response, and vice versa.

Anderson served as a secondary reference point. Whenever Anderson dropped back to form a wide back three, Livramento either moved inverted or stayed wide and deep. If Anderson remained central, Livramento positioned himself near the center-backs in the half-space, from where he could rotate forward into depth if the outside lane was free.

On the left side, full-back Hinshelwood and winger Hutchinson rotated according to the same principles as Livramento and Elliott. Hinshelwood also frequently inverted into the deeper half-space or moved wide and deep. Both full-backs, Livramento and Hinshelwood, often initiated rotations through their inverted runs when the ball was with the near-side build-up player.

Runs into depth, however, were usually triggered only when other players moved to offer passing options. The No. 10 McAtee also played an important role as a reference point. When McAtee (and/or Hutchinson) moved into the left half-space, Hinshelwood rotated oppositely into depth.

McAtee, as a left-sided No. 10, had a freer role. He oriented himself around the holding midfielders to occupy or overload the central area when needed. He also rotated positions with left winger Hutchinson. Often, McAtee initially moved far into the left half-space to pull defenders out of the No. 10 zone behind him and then sometimes rotated further back toward the central center-back position.

In response, either full-back Hinshelwood or holding midfielder Anderson rotated forward into depth. Alternatively, winger Hutchinson could rotate into the half-space, prompting full-back Hinshelwood to rotate wider.

The English rotations created difficult conditions for Germany’s man-oriented attacking pressing. Man-marking was repeatedly manipulated, which in turn stretched and opened up spaces. Thanks to the flexibility of long balls and superiority in second balls, England’s build-up play additionally benefited in the first half. This led to repeated situations resembling counter-attacks, as England had plenty of central space available after bypassing the press.

The early goal also forced Germany to press higher more frequently and reduced their tendency to drop deep. Germany’s pressing behavior against England’s build-up thus became one of the decisive factors influencing the course of the game in the first half.

Author: MH is a football aficionado at heart. His apartment resembles a football library, with shelves filled with books on the great tacticians from Rinus Michels to Pep Guardiola. Of course, the book from Spielverlagerung.de is not missing. For MH, football is not just a game, it’s a way of life. He can be found on X under Mh_sv5 and LinkedIn.

#2438. NFL Week 10 injury report: Chiefs' Kenneth Walker III ruled out, Patriots' A.J. Brown questionable

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This week in the NFL, the New England Patriots and Detroit Lions will square off in Munich, the Green Bay Packers will look to spoil Kirk Cousins' return to the Minnesota Vikings, and first place in the AFC North is on the line when the Pittsburgh Steelers battle the Cincinnati Bengals on "Sunday Night Football.''

Injuries are popping up all around the league as we enter the second half of the 2026 season, and that includes at running back. Kansas City Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker III, whose 872 rushing yards rank as the second most in the NFL this season, popped up on the injury report on Friday after tweaking his groin, causing him to not practice on the final day of the week. Walker was ruled out by the Chiefs on Saturday.

"We're feeling it out just to see. We're not going to put him at risk," Chiefs coach Andy Reid said Friday, via ESPN. "If he can go, he'll go. If he can't, he can't."

Some believe new Dallas Cowboys cornerback Joey Porter Jr.'s absence in Week 9 at the Indianapolis Colts with an ankle injury is somehow connected to his lack of a new contract in the final year of his rookie deal. However, Porter Jr. (ankle) made it clear that isn't the case on Thursday. He called his entire foot, heel and ankle "jacked up." He also said the determination on whether he will play against the San Francisco 49ers will be made after practice on Friday and based on how he feels on Sunday. Porter Jr. didn't practice on Wednesday and Thursday, but he was a limited participant on Friday. That's why the Cowboys listed him as questionable for Week 10.

"That has no, I don't even know where that narrative comes from. I get it, it's the internet. I don't really pay attention to that. I don't really care for that," Porter Jr. said after practice on Thursday. "My goal is to win games and play football. That's what I want to do. If there's any chance I can get on the field, I'm going to get on the field and do what I do best."

Below, we will break down the final injury reports for all teams set to play on Sunday, beginning with our international game in Munich, Germany

The New England Patriots have an extensive final injury report for their Week 10 game in Munich, Germany against the Detroit Lions. Running back TreVeyon Henderson (illness), cornerback Carlton Davis (knee) and center Ben Brown (knee) were all ruled out after none of the three practiced at all this week. Wide receiver A.J. Brown (ankle/knee) is questionable after being a limited practice participant all week. Running back Rhamondre Stevenson (knee) didn't practice on Wednesday, but he was a limited participant on Thursday and Friday. Safety Kevin Byrard (chest) is questionable but trending in the right direction after fully practicing on Friday following being a limited participant on both Wednesday and Thursday.

Detroit Lions All-Pro safety Kerby Joseph (knee) appeared to have a shot at returning to action in Week 10 before being ruled out on Friday. He practiced as a limited participant on Wednesday and fully on Thursday, then did not practice at all on Friday. Neither Cade Mays (ankle) nor cornerback D.J. Reed (hip) practiced at all this week. Wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown (rib) is questionable after being a limited practice participant all week.

The Kansas City Chiefs ruled out both offensive lineman Jaylon Moore (ankle) and defensive lineman Peter Woods (neck) after both didn't practice all week. They also ruled out defensive tackle Omarr Norma-Lott (knee) despite him being a limited practice participant all week. Running back Kenneth Walker III (groin) popped up on the injury report on Friday after tweaking his groin in practice. Cornerback Mansoor Delane (shoulder) is questionable despite fully practicing all week.

Wide receiver Zachariah Branch (hamstring) is the only player the Atlanta Falcons ruled out on Friday. However, they did also list linebacker Divine Deablo (forearm) as doubtful. He was a limited-practice participant before, but did not practice on Thursday or Friday. Defensive tackle Gervon Dexter Sr. (illness) and edge rusher James Pearce Jr. (back) are both questionable after each player didn't practice on Wednesday and then were limited in practice on both Thursday and Friday. Linebacker Josh Woods (ankle) is trending in the right direction: he didn't practice on Wednesday, was limited on Thursday and then fully practiced on Friday.

The Houston Texans have a lengthy final injury report. Three players were ruled out without practicing this week: Linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair (groin/personal reason), tight end Brevin Jordan (finger/foot), OL Keylan Rutledge (neck/shoulder). Edge rusher Danielle Hunter (hamstring) went the wrong way this week: he practiced fully on Wednesday, was limited on Thursday, didn't practice on Friday and was subsequently ruled out. The same goes for offensive tackle Trent Brown (illness/wrist): he practiced fully on Wednesday and Thursday before not practicing on Friday and being ruled out. Guard Wyatt Teller (back/illness) was limited twice this week and is questionable. Running back David Montgomery (groin) is trending in the right direction: he didn't practice on Wednesday, he was limited on Thursday and fully practiced on Friday.

The Cleveland Browns had a short injury report in Week 10. Both safety Ronnie Hickman Jr. (concussion) and fullback Michael Burton (calf) were both ruled out after not practicing all week. Wide receiver Denzel Boston (toe) was the only player listed as questionable, and he is trending in the right direction. Boston didn't practice on Wednesday and Thursday before being a limited participant on Friday.

The Minnesota Vikings will be without All-Pro-caliber linebacker Blake Cashman (concussion) after he only practiced in a limited capacity on Friday. Tight end T.J. Hockenson (wrist/chest), defensive tackle Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins (ankle), wide receiver Jauan Jennings (calf) and quarterback Kyler Murray (hamstring) were all ruled out after all not practicing all week. Linebacker Kyle Van Noy (calf) is questionable after only practicing in a limited fashion on Friday. Both Jordan Addison (thumb) and safety Josh Metellus (shoulder) popped up on the injury report on Friday as limited participants, and they are both questionable to play.

The Jacksonville Jaguars ruled out both safety Jessie Bates and defensive tackle Jordan Davis to allow them both to have a bye week after acquiring them via trades on Monday from the Atlanta Falcons and Philadelphia Eagles, respectively. Otherwise, they would both have had to play in 18 regular-season games. Edge rusher BJ Green II (forearm) was ruled out after fully practicing all week.

The Tennessee Titans ruled out linebacker Cody Barton (concussion), linebacker Anthony Hill Jr. (neck), defensive back Jaylon Jones (knee), guard Peter Skoronski (hamstring) and wide receiver Carnell Tate (shoulder) were all ruled out after not practicing at all this week. Running back Tyjae Spears (knee) was the only player listed as questionable, but he is trending in the right direction. He didn't practice on Wednesday, was limited on Thursday and a full participant on Friday.

The Miami Dolphins ruled out center Aaron Brewer (concussion) after he didn't practice all week. Wide receiver Jared Wayne was also ruled out after being limited on Thursday and not practicing on Friday. Cornerback Darrell Baker Jr. (knee) is the only player listed as questionable after being limited on Wednesday and Thursday before practicing fully on Friday.

The Indianapolis Colts ruled out tight end Mo Alie-Cox (gorin), linebacker Jaylon Carlies (neck), linebacker Akeem Davis-Gaither (knee), long snapper Luke Rhodes (hamstring) and offensive tackle Jalen Travis (knee) after they all didn't practice all week. Defensive tackle Jerry Tillery (calf) was ruled out after being limited on Wednesday and then not practicing the rest of the week. Edge rusher Arden Key (hamstring) is questionable after fully practicing all week, and tight end Will Mallory (hamstring) popped up on the injury report as questionable after being limited in practice on Friday.

The Carolina Panthers only ruled out one player after he didn't practice all week: linebacker Bobby Okereke (foot). Two players were listed as doubtful after being limited practice participants all week: cornerback Mike Jackson (groin) and running back Jonathon Brooks (groin). Wide receiver Xavier Legette (knee) is questionable after practicing fully all week. Edge rusher Jaelan Phillips (hamstring) is questionable after being a full practice participant on both Wednesday and Friday while being limited on Thursday. Cornerback Will Lee III (hamstring) is questionable after being limited on Friday. Offensive lineman Brady Christensen (hamstring) is questionable after being a full practice participant all week.

The Buffalo Bills didn't rule out any players, but they listed offensive tackle Spencer Brown (ankle) as doubtful after he was limited on Wednesday and didn't practice the rest of the week. Cornerback Christian Benford (wrist) is trending in the right direction after being limited on Wednesday and Thursday before being a full participant on Friday.

The New York Jets ruled out just one player after he didn't practice all week: linebacker Trevin Wallace (groin). Wide receiver Garrett Wilson (concussion) is trending in the right direction after being limited on Wednesday and Thursday before being a full participant on Friday. The same goes for wide receiver Omar Cooper Jr. (ankle), edge rusher Joseph Ossai (ankle) and cornerback Nahshon Wright (back). Wide receiver Adonai Mitchell (knee) popped up on the injury report on Friday, but he still practiced fully.

The Seattle Seahawks ruled out quarterback Sam Darnold (ribs, quadriceps), guard Quenton Nelson (knee) and defensive tackle Leonard Williams (stinger) after all three didn't practice all week. #2437. MLB rumors: Blue Jays targeting Ketel Marte, Giants rejecting trade calls for ace Logan Webb

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The annual GM Meetings came and went this week with two significant transactions. The Braves signed reliever Evan Phillips (three years and $35 million) and the Red Sox signed slugger Jake Bauers (four years and $58 million). Bauers will give Boston some sorely needed home run power. Phillips will pair with Robert Suarez in the late innings for Atlanta.

Otherwise, the GM Meetings brought a lot of rumors and presumably the groundwork was laid for moves that could be completed later this offseason. Here are our top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Saturday's hot stove happenings.

The Blue Jays have interest in Diamondbacks second baseman Ketel Marte, who has a full no-trade protection, reports Sportsnet. It does not appear a trade is imminent. We ranked Marte among the offseason's top trade candidates despite his odd AWOL incidents the last few seasons. Even at 33, he remains one of the game's best second basemen.

The Blue Jays went 79-83 this past season largely because of their offense, which ranked dead last in runs and home runs. They also ranked 17th in WAR at second base as All-Star Ernie Clement ran out of steam in the second half. Offensively, Marte is coming off his worst 162-game season since 2018, though he would still represent a clear upgrade for the Blue Jays.

The Giants continue to decline trade calls about ace righty Logan Webb, reports USA Today. Webb, 30 next week, had his worst full season in the big leagues in 2026, in part due to a nagging knee injury, though he is signed affordably through 2028. San Francisco needs to add to its rotation, not subtract one of the game's best and most durable starters.

That said, a Webb trade would presumably net the Giants multiple young players and improve the team's talent base. It never hurts to listen, but for now, the Giants seem disinclined to move their best pitcher since Madison Bumgarner was in his prime. Webb and Landen Roupp are the only locks for San Francisco's 2027 rotation at the moment.

Not surprisingly, the Braves want to add at least one starting pitcher, according to The Athletic. They could also re-sign Raisel Iglesias or bring in another late-inning reliever even after signing Phillips. Chris Sale and Grant Holmes are Atlanta's only returning healthy starters. Bryce Elder (knee), Spencer Schwellenbach (elbow) and Spencer Strider (elbow) all finished the season injured.

The Braves will give Didier Fuentes, who was so dominant as a reliever this past season, a chance to start in 2027. It will be difficult to count on him for a full season, however. Fuentes, 21, threw a career-high 97 innings between the minors, majors, and postseason in 2026. Atlanta will need to monitor his workload next year. Another starter to soak up innings is a must this offseason.

The Tigers have interest in free agent left-hander Shota Imanaga, reports MLB.com. Jackson Jobe, Troy Melton, River Ryan, and Framber Valdez are presumably locks for Detroit's rotation. Ty Madden and Keider Montero are depth options. Reese Olson is expected back from shoulder surgery early next year. Still, the Tigers could clearly use another starting pitcher.

We ranked Imanaga, 33, as the 30th-best free agent available this offseason. He has been very home run prone the last two years (1.9 homers per nine innings), which could make him a good match for what is now called Fifth Third Park. Detroit's stadium tends to play pitcher-friendly, particularly in April and September (and October), when the ball doesn't carry well in the cold.

The Blue Jays are receiving calls about infielder Ernie Clement and utility man Davis Schneider, reports The Athletic. Teams have also inquired about catcher Brandon Valenzuela, who was a Gold Glove finalist as a rookie in 2026. Toronto reportedly has interest in Jazz Chisholm Jr. as it seeks more of a power bat on the infield, potentially making Clement expendable.

Schneider, 27, had a poor 2026 and spent time in Triple-A, though he is versatile and has hit lefties in spots over the years. There is a shocking shortage of quality right-handed bats throughout baseball right now. Schneider's heavy plate discipline approach and ability to play left field as well as some infield positions make him an interesting enough target this offseason.

The Cubs, Padres, and White Sox are among several teams pursuing Japanese right-hander Kaima Taira, reports the San Diego Union-Tribune. Taira, 26, had a 1.36 ERA in 145 innings for the Seibu Lions in 2026. We ranked him as the 19th-best free agent available this offseason, though he could ultimately wind up in the bullpen given his height (5-foot-8).

The Padres and two Chicago teams need starting pitching this offseason (they need multiple starters, really) and would likely use Taira in their rotation, at least to begin the season. For what it's worth, Taira told Sanspo he does not have a preferred destination, geographically. The Cubs, Padres, and White Sox would all give him a chance to pitch for a contender right away.

The Cardinals have declined trade inquiries into first baseman Alec Burleson and shortstop Masyn Winn, according to the St. Louis Post-Dispatch. St. Louis is also receiving interest in catchers Jimmy Crooks and Pedro Pagés, who are more likely to be traded. Burleson and Winn are off-limits, though, and considered part of the long-term future in St. Louis.

Leo Bernal, who was so impressive during his September call up, and top prospect Rainiel Rodriguez are the future behind the plate for the Cardinals. Pagés is a traditional glove-first backup catcher. Crooks has some offensive upside thanks to his hard-hit ability (exit velocity, etc.), and he rates well as a pitch-framer and thrower. He's an appealing target for catcher-needy teams.

#2435. Pelicans' Dejounte Murray requests trade after venting about franchise in deleted social media posts

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New Orleans Pelicans guard Dejounte Murray wants to be traded. A day after defending himself on social media in a now-deleted post that criticized his play during a 145-111 loss to the Brooklyn Nets earlier this week, the former All-Star and his representatives requested a trade from the franchise, the team announced Friday. One team that has "registered interest" in adding Murray is the Phoenix Suns, per Chris Haynes.

"Today, Dejounte Murray's representatives informed us of his request to be traded," the team said. "We will evaluate potential trade opportunities that are in the best interest of our organization."

ProPelsTalk, a Pelicans podcast, posted clips on social media highlighting purported mistakes Murray made during his team's fourth consecutive loss, to which Murray responded that fans have "no f--- ing clue what we are dealing with."

"Ohhhhh let's talk about it," Murray posted in a now-deleted tweet. "When you run post plays, are they suppose to catch on the block or the 3pt line? Let's hear it Mr social media coach, Gm and President? You have no f---ing clue what we dealing with. Maybe you should ask the whole team individually how they feel on a serious note and then pull rethink alot of shit."

Murray finished with five points, four assists, and two rebounds in 28 minutes during the loss. This season, Murray is averaging 13.4 points, the lowest since his third season in the league with the San Antonio Spurs. On the same day Murray tweeted and then deleted that tweet, he also responded to another tweet, noting that the Pelicans are 1-8 with Murray and 3-0 without him.

"From what's going on INSIDE, this sounds like someone hit you to say this!!" Murray wrote in a now-deleted tweet. "THE 'SABOTAGE' IS REAL!!"

Murray appeared in just 14 games during the 2025-26 season after recovering from a torn Achilles that sidelined him for more than a year. The Athletic's Sam Amick reported on Thursday that he expects the Pelicans to have "very legitimate conversations" about Murray being moved.

"Dejounte (Murray), I would fully expect to have very legitimate conversations about him being on the move," Amick said. I thought that would be the case closer to the deadline. The mood certainly is the type of thing that could accelerate it."

Murray, 30, is in the final guaranteed season of his current contract. He has a player option for $30.7 million for the 2027-28 season.

#2434. What's next for Red Sox after Jake Bauers deal? Plus more intel from the MLB GM Meetings

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

LAS VEGAS — Uncertainty permeated the ARIA Resort & Casino throughout this week's MLB GM Meetings. The looming lockout, of course, played a major role in all of this.

With Dec. 1  approaching, media, executives, and all within the baseball industry had some questions: what would baseball look like once the inevitable lockout goes into place? What will it look like once it returns? How do you build a roster with such indeterminacy?

For the Red Sox, a small piece of this peculiar period centers on what to do with former top prospect Kristian Campbell.

Tuesday (Nov. 17) is a significant date, marking the deadline for teams to decide which players to protect from the Rule 5 draft by adding them to their 40-man roster. Campbell, who did not appear in a big-league game in 2026, is currently on the 40-man, signing an eight-year $60 million extension just eight games into his 2025 rookie campaign. But after his demotion in late June of that season, Campbell never found his way back to the majors.

Now, with the lockout upon baseball, according to one source familiar with the situation, Campbell's 40-man spot might be in jeopardy.

Boston is weighing the possibility of designating Campbell for assignment. When Craig Breslow, the Sox's president of baseball operations, was asked about that Tuesday, he brushed aside the question.

"I'm not going to speak to that right now," he said "Kristian's part of our organization. We're really happy about that, and we are invested in doing everything we can to get him to perform like he's capable of."

Now, if the Red Sox do DFA Campbell, the belief is that he would clear waivers, given his contract and lackluster performance at the minor-league level. Campbell is owed $55 million over the next six seasons, earning $13 million and $16 million over the 2031 and 2032 seasons, respectively. Campbell posted a .256/.383/.380 slash line with eight homers in 462 plate appearances at Triple-A in 2026.

Because of those figures, one league executive suggested during the GM Meetings that their club would have no interest in Campbell. The exec took it a step further, confidently suggesting that they couldn't envision any team claiming the outfielder, considering the contract.

Hypothetically, if Campbell is DFA'd, the Red Sox would free up a 40-man roster spot. If he clears waivers, Campbell, who has less than a year of MLB service time, would be outrighted to Triple-A Worcester. The Red Sox could then eventually add him back to the 40-man roster once they feel his production is worthy of another promotion to the parent club.

None of this would provide the Red Sox with any financial relief unless another team were to claim him. Campbell's contract would still count toward their competitive balance tax payroll even if he were removed from the 40-man roster and remained in the minors.

The risk-reward of such a move is something the Red Sox will also have to consider. Campbell has already acknowledged losing confidence following his recent struggles at both the major- and minor-league levels.

"He's got a world of potential," said Breslow. "We saw it in the minor leagues when he was coming up. We saw it in the first part of the season in [2025]. Then I think we started to see it in the second half last year, too, [at Worcester]. I still feel like he has a really bright big-league career ahead of him, and excited to get into spring training and see that manifest on the field."

The Red Sox signed Jake Bauers to a four-year, $58 million deal Friday, giving the club another power bat in their lineup. Willson Contreras will continue to anchor first base while Bauers will serve as the primary DH, filling in for Contreras from time to time.

Bauers had a breakout season with the Brewers this year, batting .266/.389/.484 with an .874 OPS and 26 homers. The combo of plate discipline and damage in the strike zone intrigued the Red Sox. Furthermore, his ability to lift the ball in the air and use the entire field despite being a lefty gives the Red Sox confidence that he will be productive at Fenway.

With Bauers part of the fold, though, Jarren Duran's future with the club is even more murky. The Sox are a heavily left-handed offensive club with Bauers, Wilyer Abreu, Masataka Yoshida, Roman Anthony, and Duran in the mix.

One is likely going to have to go. And Duran, who could earn upwards of $11 million in arbitration next season, appears to be the most likely to be dealt.

Even before the Bauers signing, multiple sources suggested during the GM Meetings that both the Red Sox and Duran might be better off parting ways via trade.

"I've been hearing for three years now about the outfield logjam that we have, but the reality is we haven't had all of our outfielders, including Masataka, healthy at the same time," Breslow said. "These things have largely taken care of themselves, unfortunately."

#2433. NFL Week 10 last-minute picks, best bets: Chiefs, Steelers take advantage of schedule quirk

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Quarterbacks are the story pretty much every week in the NFL, but Week 10 has several fascinating storylines developing under center. For instance, three are set to make their first career starts on Sunday in rookies Fernando Mendoza and Carson Beck along with second-year quarterback Kyle McCord. On top of that, Kirk Cousins is set to start in his return to Minnesota after being acquired at the trade deadline, as will Jacoby Brissett, who the Ravens dealt for to help cushion the blow of losing Lamar Jackson.

As you can see by simply looking at this shakeup at quarterback, the aftermath of the trade deadline is going to have ripple effects that spread through the entire league. Naturally, that adds another element for bettors to consider as they put together their picks for Week 10. To help sort through the madness of the last week, we've put together some last-minute best bets for the slate along with picks for every other game on the docket.

Note: Chicago, Denver, Philadelphia, and Tampa Bay are on the bye in Week 10.

There's arguably no offense hotter right now than the Bengals. Over their four-game winning streak, they've averaged over 35 points per game, and Joe Burrow has been playing at an MVP level. The Cincinnati QB has 18 total touchdowns over this stretch and a 132.0 passer rating. Simply put, they've been a bulldozer. However, I do think it's worth pointing out who they've played over the course of the winning streak: at Dolphins, at Ravens (no Lamar Jackson), vs. Titans and vs. Falcons. Not exactly a murderer's row.

Pittsburgh, who beat these Bengals back in Week 3, should provide much more resistance than what they've faced recently. The Steelers defense is tied for the fifth-lowest yards-per-play average (5.0), tied for the fourth-lowest points-per-game allowed (18.0), and tied for the eighth-lowest passer rating allowed (83.3). Meanwhile, Cincinnati's defense is tied for the most yards per rush attempt allowed so far this season (5.0), which sets up Jaylen Warren to continue his ascent as one of the true breakout players of the season.

On top of this being a potential mismatch for the Bengals going up against this stout Steelers team, their scheduling surrounding this game does them no favors either. While they'll be at home in Week 10, Cincinnati is coming off an international game in Madrid last week. As for the Steelers, they're fresh off their bye week, creating a sizable rest discrepancy. All of this is a recipe for an upset.

Projected score: Steelers 27, Bengals 24The pick: Steelers +3.5

While their 3-5 records don't exactly scream playoff contenders, first place in the NFC South is on the line in this game. Bryce Young doesn't have the best history going up against the Saints, as the Panthers quarterback is just 1-5 against his division foe in his career. That said, I think there's a window here for him to get a rare victory against New Orleans on Sunday.

While his numbers have come down since his stellar start to begin the season, Young started to look more like himself in the loss to Denver, completing 71.7% of his passes to go along with three touchdowns. The Saints secondary is allowing 7.3 yards per attempt so far this season, which is tied for the fifth-highest in the league. Their 99.5 passer rating allowed is also the seventh-highest in the NFL. This isn't as daunting a matchup for Young, who had to face Tampa Bay, Green Bay, and Denver over Carolina's recent three-game losing streak. I like him to rebound here.

Meanwhile, New Orleans is 1-4 straight-up and 0-5 ATS at home this season, so the Superdome hasn't been too friendly thus far.

Projected score: Panthers 24, Saints 21The pick: Panthers +2.5

Similar to what we discussed with Cincinnati, the Falcons do have to play immediately the following week after an international game in Madrid last Sunday. That may only put them further behind the eight ball against a Chiefs team that cruised to a 35-12 win over the Jets last week. Patrick Mahomes did give us all a scare in the midst of that game after injuring his elbow, but it's not serious enough to keep him out of this matchup.

Mahomes has thrown five touchdowns and no interceptions over his past two games, but his lack of a downfield threat has been noticeable. He's averaging an NFL-low 5.6 air yards per attempt this season as the Chiefs have really looked for pass catches to put up yards after the catch. Well, they just acquired some help in that regard in Josh Downs, whom they brought in before the deadline in a trade with the Colts. The wideout has a knack for creating separation and now has a capable quarterback to deliver the football to him, so Kansas City could see quick dividends from this addition. That's especially true against a Falcons secondary that was just lit up by the Bengals last week and just traded away star safety Jessie Bates III to the Jaguars.

Atlanta is also 0-4 straight-up and ATS in its last four games against the AFC.

Projected score: Chiefs 26, Falcons 20The pick: Chiefs -3

While they won't play this weekend, Jacksonville went all-in at the deadline, making trades to acquire Jessie Bates III, Jordan Davis and Davon Godchaux to bolster its defense for a potential Super Bowl run. On the flip side, Tennessee traded away pieces, including standout safety Amani Hooker and, going back a couple of weeks, defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons. That's a lot of talent being drained from the defense, which doesn't bode well against Trevor Lawrence, who is making a sneaky MVP push. Entering Week 10, his 111.7 passer rating ranks second among quarterbacks who have started at least eight games, only looking up to Burrow.

As this double-digit spread suggests, this is a David vs. Goliath matchup, and it's hard to imagine the underdog keeping this thing close. Even before making these trades, Jacksonville's defense was allowing 15.1 points per game (second-best in the NFL) and has also allowed 20 or fewer points in six straight road games. Tony Pollard, who remained with the team through the deadline, has been a bright spot in Tennessee's offense in recent weeks, but could be negated here. The Jaguars are allowing 3.7 yards per carry this season, along with an average of 89.3 rushing yards allowed per game that ranks fifth-lowest in the NFL.

A blowout is brewing in this matchup in favor of Jacksonville, who is 13-3 ATS over its last 16 games with a +16.3 points per game differential.

Projected score: Jaguars 34, Titans 16The pick: Jaguars -10.5

Welcome to the NFL, Fernando Mendoza. The No. 1 overall pick at the 2026 NFL Draft is set to make his first career start in the aftermath of the Raiders trading Kirk Cousins, who started the first nine games of the year, to Minnesota before the deadline. This will be a baptism by fire for the Indiana product as he'll face off against a Seattle defense that is among the very best in the NFL. The Seahawks are allowing a league-low 244.2 total yards per game entering Week 10, along with an average of 18.0 points per game allowed that is tied for fourth-fewest. That just feels like too tall a mountain to climb for Mendoza right out of the gate.

Meanwhile, the Raiders defense won't do their young quarterback any favors. They're currently on a six-game streak of allowing 30-plus points, which is tied for the longest streak within a season all-time. So, even with Sam Darnold (quad) sidelined and backup Drew Lock set to play through an oblique injury, the Seattle offense should find plenty of scoring opportunities. This could be a breakout game for Zach Charbonnet after leading the team with 16 carries last week for 77 yards, as the Raiders are allowing an NFL-high 5.0 yards per carry.

Given that Mendoza is getting the start, it's also worth pointing out that No. 1 overall quarterbacks are 1-15-1 straight up and 3-14 ATS in their first career starts since 2003.

Conversion rate has statistically been proven to be one of the best indicators for predicting a team’s success (Souza et al., 2019). All the more astonishing, then, that the underlying influencing factors are still largely unknown to most, leaving chance conversion for many as something of a black box. This analysis aims to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of goalscoring situations.

Chance conversion is most often associated with mental aspects. Accordingly, after defeats it is sometimes used as an excuse, partly due to a lack of more convincing alternative explanations. After all, the coach is said to have little or no influence on the psychological state of his players. Instead, the players are expected to learn how to better handle the pressure of a goalscoring opportunity, and in doing so become more efficient in front of goal.
